datums-and-hole-position-on-circular-mac.seoTitle: Bolt Circle Diameter and Hole Position on CNC Parts
datums-and-hole-position-on-circular-mac.heading: Bolt Circle Diameter and Hole Position on CNC Parts
datums-and-hole-position-on-circular-mac.description: Why can a flange with the right bolt circle still fail to fit? Relate hole position, the locating bore and pattern clocking to the assembly and inspection.
datums-and-hole-position-on-circular-mac.intro: A flange hole position tolerance must be interpreted with the specified locating references. A flange can have the right hole diameters and bolt circle yet refuse to fit its mating part. The missing information is often the relationship between the pattern, the locating bore and the seating face. Start with how the assembly locates the flange; that determines which dimensions and geometric controls matter.
datums-and-hole-position-on-circular-mac.libraryTitle: Bolt circles, datums and flange fit
datums-and-hole-position-on-circular-mac.summary: Why a correct bolt-circle diameter does not establish the complete mounting pattern.
datums-and-hole-position-on-circular-mac.reader_question: How do I specify a circular hole pattern so the flange fits its mating part?

sections.title: Functional datums on a flange
sections.html:
Flange datum selection should follow the contacts that locate the installed part. Pilot bore alignment matters for a cover that slides over a housing pilot and seats against a flat face. The pilot locates it radially, the face establishes its axial position, and the bolts hold it down. In that arrangement, the mounting holes need enough clearance for assembly while their pattern remains related to the pilot. Making each bolt hole a close locating fit can introduce competing constraints.

A dowel-located plate is different: the dowels may control position and orientation while a large central opening merely provides clearance. The most prominent circle in the face view is therefore not automatically the right datum feature. A functional datum scheme follows the contacts that locate the part in use.

The circular machined-part reference shows a central opening, stepped bores and smaller face holes. On your drawing, identify which features locate, retain or clear the mating assembly, so machining and inspection use the same references.

sections.title: What does a bolt-circle diameter tell you?
sections.html:
Pitch-circle diameter, or PCD, is also called bolt circle diameter. It defines the nominal circle through the hole centers. Hole size, pattern orientation, allowable position error and the relationship to a locating bore require separate callouts.

RequirementAssembly question it answers
Hole diameter and size limitsWill the fastener or mating pin fit within the permitted size range?
PCD, hole count and spacingWhere are the hole centers in the nominal layout?
Position control and datum referencesHow much variation is permitted relative to the locating features?
Angular referenceHow is the pattern oriented relative to a port, key or other asymmetric feature?
Face, shoulder and axis controlsHow must the seating surfaces and locating axis relate?

Calculating PCD from equally spaced holes

For a nominal pattern of n ≥ 2 equally spaced holes, the adjacent center-to-center distance c is a chord: PCD = c / sin(180° / n). Angles are in degrees. As a hypothetical layout example, four equally spaced holes on a 40 mm PCD have an adjacent-center distance of 40 × sin(45°) ≈ 28.28 mm. Opposite centers are 40 mm apart.

PCD calculation from hole spacing assumes equally spaced bolt holes with their centers on one ideal circle. It is useful when interpreting a nominal layout or comparing a sample with a drawing, but it does not evaluate actual hole position, axis orientation or compliance with a geometric tolerance. Edge-to-edge caliper measurements also need the hole diameters accounted for before they can represent center distance.

Interpret coordinate errors in the declared alignment

Hole position tolerance must be interpreted in the declared alignment and drawing convention. For this limited two-dimensional diagnostic at one cross-section, the diametrical position error is 2√(Δx² + Δy²), twice the radial distance from the nominal hole centre in the declared coordinate system.

As a hypothetical arithmetic example, offsets of 0.03 mm in X and 0.04 mm in Y give a radial offset of 0.05 mm and a diametrical value of 0.10 mm. Comparing each coordinate separately with ±0.08 mm would answer a different question from comparing a 0.10 mm diametrical value with a specified 0.08 mm position zone.

This cross-section example leaves hole-axis orientation, depth, material-condition modifiers and datum mobility outside the calculation. Evaluate a production control frame under its stated drawing standard and full measurement procedure. A coordinate spreadsheet can help diagnose an offset while the released requirement determines acceptance.

sections.title: Pattern clocking around a port or key
sections.html:
A six-hole pattern repeats every 60 degrees, but the rest of the component may not. Suppose a side port must face upward when the flange is installed. Rotating the holes relative to that port changes the assembly even when the PCD, hole count and equal spacing remain correct. Hole pattern clocking connects the pattern to the port through an identified angular reference feature.

With a rotationally interchangeable mating component, that extra orientation requirement may serve no function. Unnecessary clocking controls can make production and inspection harder without improving the assembly. The designer needs to distinguish a genuinely oriented interface from a symmetric one.

Hole axes matter through the thickness as well. A center position at one face alone cannot describe the orientation of a long dowel hole. The drawing standard and selected controls must represent the engagement required by the mating feature. Position, concentricity and runout evaluate different characteristics and cannot simply be substituted for one another.

The report passes, but the flange will not fit

First identify the report's origin and angular orientation, then compare them with the assembly contacts. Alignment to an outside diameter can miss the required relationship to a separate pilot bore. Check for a changed mating part, burr or finish buildup before enlarging holes. If the pilot or seating surface is involved, also check the fit and runout specification.

sections.title: Transferring the locating axis into another setup
sections.html:
Flange machining datum transfer is important when a turned pilot and milled holes require more than one operation. Thin ring workholding adds a support question because holding forces can change the shape used for the next setup. Repositioning is practical when the next setup locates from suitable features and retains the relationships on the drawing. The number of setups alone does not establish whether a route will satisfy the part.

A finished face and bore can provide locating references for later work, provided they are accessible and can tolerate the holding method. A thin ring presents another problem: clamping can change its shape. If the assembly restrains the ring, the specification needs to distinguish the installed condition from the free condition, and inspection needs the corresponding support arrangement.

Recessed holes also require room for the cutter, holder and measuring probe. A short hole behind a tall surrounding wall can be harder to reach than a deeper hole on an open face. The complete model and section views make that obstruction visible during CNC milling review. Permitted radii or local relief can then be considered against the mating geometry.

sections.title: What should the inspection report show?
sections.html:
A flange inspection report should identify the drawing revision, controlled features and evaluation alignment. CMM alignment for hole patterns must follow the required references so the reported coordinates answer the assembly question. For a pilot-located flange, the relevant results relate the mounting pattern to the specified locating axis and seating face. Hole diameters remain necessary, but they answer only the size question.

Hexagon’s introduction to coordinate metrology explains how a part coordinate system relates measured features to its datums and how alignment connects it to the measuring machine. This is why an alignment description belongs beside the reported coordinates. A CMM’s presence alone says nothing about which requirements were evaluated.

For repeated assembly acceptance, a defined functional gauge may be useful when it represents the released requirement. A convenient mating part is less informative if its own dimensions, revision and wear are uncontrolled. It can show an assembly symptom without proving every drawing characteristic.

Surface treatment adds a timing question. A coated bore and a masked seating face may require different process measurements, while final acceptance concerns the completed condition. The controlled drawing and report should make those stages distinguishable.

Investigate the assembly symptom before changing the holes
ObservationCheck firstUseful evidence
All holes appear displaced togetherOrigin, pilot identification and datum alignment.Report alignment and the same revision as the mating part.
One or two holes fail to line upThose hole axes, local burrs and the measured pattern.Individual feature results and edge condition.
Pattern fits only after rotationClocking reference and any asymmetric port or key.The defined angular relationship and assembled orientation.
Bolts start but bind through the flangeHole-axis direction, engagement depth and mating geometry.Checks covering the required depth and installed configuration.

Record the alignment with the feature results. Recentring every pattern on its own best-fit circle can hide the relationship to a separate locating bore when the drawing requires that bore as a reference.

Use the turned-interface measurement review when the symptom also involves the flange pilot or seating shoulder. That keeps a hole-pattern correction from concealing a different fitted-surface problem.

sections.title: Release the relationship the assembly needs
sections.html:
The release package for a pilot-located flange needs the locating bore and fit, flange mounting face, complete mounting pattern and any angular reference. Finished hole pattern inspection should evaluate that relationship in the specified final condition. Depths and shoulders then establish where the mating components sit. The model shows the form; the controlled drawing defines the permitted variation and applicable drawing standard.

Material, final treatment and restricted clamp contacts complete the manufacturing context. Where receiving inspection needs recorded pattern results or a functional gauge, the release also identifies the measurement condition and scope. Those details allow a supplier to quote the same part that the receiving team intends to accept.

If the pilot, bolt pattern or mating component changes, revisit the relationship as a whole. Carrying an old PCD note onto a revised assembly is easy; preserving the intended locating arrangement requires the references and acceptance basis to follow the revision.

what-matters-when-ordering-a-custom-inde.seoTitle: Custom Indexing Plungers: Fit, Stroke and Spring Force
what-matters-when-ordering-a-custom-inde.heading: Custom Indexing Plungers: Fit, Stroke and Spring Force
what-matters-when-ordering-a-custom-inde.description: Specify a custom indexing plunger from its installed position. Relate pin fit, projection, engagement and retraction to spring behavior and assembly scope.
what-matters-when-ordering-a-custom-inde.intro: A pin that reaches a hole on the bench may stop short once its body is mounted. A custom indexing plunger needs enough engagement in the working position and enough retraction to clear the moving part. Show the body, mating hole and operating clearance together in a section through the installed mechanism.
what-matters-when-ordering-a-custom-inde.libraryTitle: Custom indexing plungers and installed fit
what-matters-when-ordering-a-custom-inde.summary: Pin engagement, withdrawal and spring behavior in the mounted mechanism.
what-matters-when-ordering-a-custom-inde.reader_question: How do I specify an indexing plunger that engages and releases correctly after installation?

sections.title: How closely should the pin fit its mating hole?
sections.html:
A custom indexing plunger needs an indexing pin fit suited to its locating function. A close pin-and-hole fit can improve repeatable location when aligned, while leaving less room for misalignment during engagement. A mechanism that moves into position with some variation may need a different clearance or entry geometry. The right choice follows the locating function and operating conditions.

Indexing plunger mounting depth sets the reach from the installed body reference. Mating hole alignment also depends on the approach direction established by the body mount. Even a correctly sized pin can bind when that direction misses the mating-hole axis. A section and assembly view therefore need to relate the pin, body and mating hole, including any movement or deflection relevant to engagement.

The LZZ indexing-plunger reference illustrates a projecting pin and mounted body. It does not provide an application load rating or operating-life result. Those requirements depend on the complete mechanism and need their own definition.

Is an indexing plunger the same as a ball plunger?

An indexing pin enters a mating hole to a defined engagement depth. A ball plunger has a different contact and release geometry. The phrase “spring plunger” is too broad to establish interchangeable behavior. When replacing a catalog item, its identification and installed function are more useful than matching the outside thread alone.

sections.title: Should the pin return automatically or stay retracted?
sections.html:
For a locking indexing plunger, state whether the pin should return toward engagement when released or remain in a stay-retracted position. Automatic return suits a mechanism in which the operator releases the pin to engage it. A rest position is useful when the moving member must travel while the pin stays out of the way. The mechanism must also provide a deliberate way to leave that rest position and return the pin.

Ganter’s GN 413 information gives a concrete example: its rest-position versions retain the withdrawn pin by rotating the pull ring into a notch. That describes the cited standard product. Its dimensions, spring values and load information do not establish the performance of a custom LZZ assembly.

Installed access can decide whether a suitable mechanism is usable. A pull ring may need space above the body; a rest-position action may need room to turn. A surrounding guard or retaining nut can obstruct that movement even though the pin itself has sufficient stroke. The operating envelope belongs in the assembly review.

sections.title: Dimensional checks and functional tests
sections.html:
A dimensional report records the pin diameter, body thread and specified travel geometry. Return force, load capacity and operating life require separate acceptance evidence.

RequirementUseful acceptance basisEssential limit
Pin and mating fitSize limits, working length and alignment in the specified condition.A fit result alone does not establish load capacity.
Body mountingThread definition, seating reference and controlled installed depth.The same body can give a different reach at a different mounting depth.
Withdrawal and returnTravel and clearance in the mounted configuration; stated rest behavior.Loose-component movement can miss an installed obstruction.
Spring forcePermitted force at identified working positions and measurement conditions.One force value does not describe the whole stroke.
Load or operating lifeA separately defined calculation or test, configuration and responsibility.A machining quotation does not imply that qualification is included.

The component drawings and functional acceptance instruction need compatible revisions. A spring substitution can change operating force while leaving the outer dimensions unchanged; a body-depth change can alter engagement without changing the spring.

Test the actions in the mounted arrangement

  1. An installed functional test should mount the body to the defined seating reference and depth, including the specified nut or retaining method. Indexing plunger spring force must be evaluated at the stated working positions and conditions.
  2. Check full working engagement and complete withdrawal at the required mating positions.
  3. Measure operating force at the stated stroke positions and direction, with the agreed lubrication and conditions.
  4. Check return and any stay-retracted action without obstruction from surrounding hardware.

The Ganter GN 413 table reports initial and end spring loads separately on its standard products. A custom acceptance instruction similarly needs its force positions defined. Values and load capacity from that catalogue remain specific to the cited products.

If the application expects the pin to be released while carrying a lateral load, define that condition with the responsible designer. The spring return force alone cannot establish the release force, resistance to binding or structural capacity of the complete mechanism.

sections.title: Projection, engagement and retraction stroke
sections.html:
Indexing plunger projection is the distance the pin extends from a defined body reference in a stated position. Engagement is how much of the pin enters the mating feature after installation. Indexing plunger stroke should be specified as the usable movement available to pull the pin back. A gap between body and mating part consumes some projection before engagement begins.

For a hypothetical rigid, coaxial arrangement, assume the pin projects 8 mm beyond the body face and the mating plate begins 3 mm away. The geometric penetration is 8 − 3 = 5 mm, provided the hole is deep enough. To leave the tip 1 mm clear of the near face of the plate, the withdrawn projection must be at most 3 − 1 = 2 mm. The required retraction is therefore at least 8 − 2 = 6 mm.

This is a nominal geometry example, not a product rating or tolerance analysis. Actual limits must include dimensional variation, mounting adjustment, deflection and any lead-in that does not count as working engagement. Moving the body closer to the plate increases reach, but it also changes the withdrawal clearance.

Separate the lead-in from working engagement

A chamfered nose can start entering a hole before the working pin length is engaged. The assembly section should show which region provides the required engagement and where the tip sits when withdrawn. A barely entering nose should not be mistaken for the accepted engaged position.

Check engagement and withdrawal at opposite tolerance limits

Define P as the projection to the pin tip, G as the installed gap to the mating part, and N as the nose length that does not provide the required full working engagement. For a rigid, coaxial arrangement, a first worst-case check is minimum working engagement = Pmin − Gmax − Nmax. Sufficient usable hole depth is also required.

The retraction clearance requirement should be checked separately from minimum working engagement. If the tip must withdraw a clearance C behind the near face of the mating part, the geometric minimum retraction requirement is Pmax − Gmin + C. Compare that requirement with the minimum usable travel of the installed mechanism. Stops, handle access and retaining hardware can reduce travel available in practice.

The rigid, coaxial calculations leave misalignment, deflection, wear and movement under load to a separate allowance or assessment. A longer projecting pin can improve engagement while making withdrawal clearance harder to achieve.

sections.title: Components included in a custom plunger
sections.html:
Define the indexing plunger assembly scope in the quotation. For a spring-loaded indexing pin, specify who supplies the spring, handle and retainers. An order for the machined pin and body leaves the remaining components and assembly under the customer's control; a complete plunger includes the agreed purchased components and functional assembly work.

The pin and body can have different material and surface requirements. A treatment suitable for the body exterior may change a close sliding interface. The accepted final condition therefore includes the working surfaces after the complete finish route, together with any lubrication or cleanliness requirement specified for the application.

Wear, corrosion exposure and service temperature can influence material selection, but a material name alone cannot establish suitability for all operating conditions. The relevant grade, condition and service requirements belong with each component definition. CNC turning review covers the machined features; any assembled-force, load or cycle evaluation needs an explicit scope and acceptance procedure.

sections.title: First-assembly approval and repeat orders
sections.html:
Repeat plunger orders should retain the accepted installed position, working engagement, withdrawal clearance and return or rest behavior. An indexing plunger load rating requires its supporting assessment or test. Dimensional approval can remain useful while that work is open, with the unresolved application load test recorded in the release.

The controlled package brings together the pin and body drawings, mating-hole definition, included hardware and any functional procedure. Its record needs to identify the actual configuration used. If mounting depth or retaining hardware changes during the trial, that accepted arrangement becomes part of the next release.

Record completed dimensional checks and outstanding application tests separately in the sample approval record. Use the accepted drawings, configuration and trial adjustments as the basis for the repeat order.

cnc-process-selection.seoTitle: CNC Milling, Turning or 5-Axis: Choosing a Practical Route
cnc-process-selection.heading: Which machining route suits your part?
cnc-process-selection.description: Choose between turning, milling, indexed 3+2 and simultaneous 5-axis machining by following the working features, tool access and inspection requirements.
cnc-process-selection.intro: A round body can need milling, and a block with a large bore can still be a milling job. The useful starting point is the relationship between the surfaces that make the part work. From there, the route has to provide cutting access, a stable way to hold the material and a way to measure the finished result.
cnc-process-selection.summary: Follow the working features to compare turning, milling and multi-axis access.
cnc-process-selection.reader_question: Which machining route can produce my working features without losing their required relationship?

sections.title: Begin with the features that locate the part
sections.html:
CNC machining process selection starts with the features that locate the part. In a CNC milling vs turning comparison, a shaft often begins with an axis as its main reference. For a housing, a mounting face and locating holes may establish the assembly position. The complete part may still need several operations.

GeometryUseful starting routeThe next question
Diameters, bores and shoulders about an axisTurningHow will flats, slots or off-axis holes relate to that axis?
Pockets, mounting faces and distributed holesMillingCan the cutter reach each feature from practical holding positions?
Angled faces or changing surface directionsIndexed or simultaneous multi-axis reviewCan each cut use a fixed direction, or must orientation change during cutting?

The turning, milling and five-axis machining reviews use the drawing and model to develop that starting idea into a route. Stock size, material, quantity and final acceptance can change the result.

sections.title: Round features and flat features can share one part
sections.html:
A stepped shaft or sleeve is a natural turning candidate because several surfaces share the rotating workpiece's axis. A keyway or clocked flat then introduces a milling operation. Its position relative to the turned surfaces becomes part of the job.

With a block or housing, the surrounding faces often make milling the more practical starting point, even when one recess is circular. The prismatic-part study and pocketed enclosure study show forms where the remaining material and accessible faces matter to holding.

Consider a hypothetical flanged sleeve with a side slot. Turning can create the bore and flange, while milling creates the slot. If the slot locates a mating key, the drawing needs its relationship to the bore and a clocking reference. The route then has to preserve that relationship when the part moves to the next operation.

sections.title: Fixed cutting directions or a changing tool angle?
sections.html:
A 3-axis vs 5-axis machining review should identify the cutting directions each feature needs. Three-axis milling can complete many parts through several holding orientations. A rotary axis can present additional faces. Indexed 3+2 machining uses two rotary directions to set an orientation, then holds that orientation while the linear axes cut. Simultaneous 5-axis machining coordinates rotary and linear motion during the path.

Rapid Axis describes the indexed and simultaneous distinction. Several angled holes may each allow a fixed cutting direction, while a blade passage may need the approach to change as the cutter advances.

Grouping related features into fewer manual setups can reduce datum transfers. It can also require more preparation, a different fixture or additional clearance. For a short run, several straightforward setups may suit the part; a repeat batch may justify another arrangement. The cost guide explains how shared preparation and repeated work affect that comparison.

An impeller model makes the access question concrete. The blade surface, neighboring blade, hub and complete tool assembly all belong in the review.

Ask what the rotary axis does during the cut

In 4-axis CNC machining, the rotary axis can index a cylindrical part to fixed positions or rotate during a coordinated cut. An indexed sleeve with four cross-holes can use fixed approaches, while a continuous wrapped feature needs the appropriate coordinated path. The complete geometry and fixture determine the viable choice.

In 3+2 work, two rotary axes establish successive fixed cutting orientations, as described in Autodesk's 3+2 roughing documentation. The quotation should identify which surfaces are cut at fixed orientations and which, if any, require simultaneous motion.

sections.title: A second setup can preserve the required relationship
sections.html:
The two-stage milling study records two operations on one component. For a new part, machining datum transfer and cross-setup dimensional control depend on how the second operation locates from references created or used in the first.

Suppose a hypothetical bracket needs a top pocket and a side hole. The first operation can leave a suitable face for locating the second, provided that face remains accessible and the fixture supports the part. The side hole's position is then evaluated from the drawing datums, with the temporary machining contacts understood as part of the process.

Some exterior surfaces may have no close relationship to the working hole. Giving them independent, appropriate limits keeps the close control on the interfaces that need it. A later design change that moves the hole or removes a locating face can alter the route even when the outside envelope barely changes.

sections.title: Carry the axis into the secondary milling operation
sections.html:
The turning followed by milling study connects a cylindrical form with secondary machining. A comparable new part needs a definition of both the milled features and their relationship to the axis and locating face.

For a flange, this may be a mounting pattern located from a bore. For a shaft, it may be a flat oriented to another feature. Diameter and slot-width results alone leave the assembly relationship untested. The datum scheme gives machining and inspection a common reference.

Turning then milling can suit a component whose off-axis features relate to its turned axis. A mill-turn machining route can reduce some transfers, while separate machines can also provide a suitable sequence. The comparison belongs at the same revision, quantity, finished condition and inspection scope so the offers describe equivalent parts.

sections.title: Allow room for the holder and the rotating fixture
sections.html:
In the multi-face machining study, a rotary setup provides approaches to several faces. Access has to include the holder, spindle approach, supports and rotating workpiece as well as the cutter tip.

Check CNC tool holder clearance against the surrounding geometry throughout the approach. Rotary fixture clearance also matters: an angled hole reachable on the bare model may be covered by a jaw in the actual setup. A different holding arrangement may expose it while hiding an underside face. These trade-offs explain why multi-axis work can still need another setup.

Fixed-angle faces and continuously changing contours raise different motion questions. The complete model allows the supplier to evaluate both against the available working space, fixture clearance and required checks.

sections.title: Deep pockets and thin walls change the route
sections.html:
Deep pocket tool reach is restricted by the opening, tool diameter and usable projection. Thin wall workholding adds a support constraint as material is removed from around that recess. Turning the part can improve the approach direction, but the opening and internal radii still constrain the cutter. Sandvik Coromant's guidance on closed pockets explains the relationship between pocket angles and tool selection.

A larger permitted corner radius or a local relief can help when the mating component allows it. Such a change belongs with the design owner. A round end mill still leaves an internal radius, regardless of the number of machine axes.

The enclosure form also illustrates what remains after the cavity is cut. Thin walls need support as the surrounding stock disappears, and a flexible part may change shape after release from the fixture. The drawing can distinguish free-state acceptance from a specified restrained condition.

Blind threads and intersecting bores need depth and access definitions. Starting with a cast housing adds a further constraint: sufficient stock must exist at the finished features in the required datum alignment.

sections.title: Compare routes against the finished requirements
sections.html:
A machining route comparison needs the same drawing limits for each offer. Finished part inspection then establishes whether the proposed route has delivered those requirements in the specified state. Geometry, material, workholding, treatment and measurement determine how a proposed process can meet them. Axis count alone provides none of those acceptance results.

Cross-setup dimensions deserve attention because they connect operations. A bore and a side hole may each be the right size while their relationship remains wrong. The critical drawing features guide follows those requirements into a measurable record.

Treated interfaces need a defined acceptance stage. A masked bore and an anodized outside face have different process needs; the material and finish guide explains the local definition. A change in quantity can also justify different workholding, so first-part approval should identify the route and checks that support the later release.

Comparing two suppliers' routes

When comparing separate turning and milling with mill-turn machining, trace the secondary features from the same required axis and face in both offers. Compare preparation, protected surfaces, treatment and final results. The RFQ inputs establish a common quotation basis.

The fixture belongs in the access review

A route proposal should show the jaws, supports, temporary stock and any rotary table alongside the part in each setup. For a contoured impeller, clearance must hold along the complete cutter-and-holder path, as discussed in the impeller guide. Any proposed change to a controlled surface remains a design decision.

Compare two process proposals on the same finished component
QuestionA useful responseWhat it resolves
Where does the first setup locate?Stock or finished contacts and the surfaces left accessible.Whether enough support and stock remain.
How does the next operation find the working axis or face?The locating feature carried into that setup.How cross-setup dimensions are preserved.
What still needs finishing after unclamping?The remaining surface, support and locating method.Whether the proposal includes a complete part.
How is the final relationship checked?Specified datums, measurement state and report scope.Whether the routes deliver equivalent acceptance evidence.

For a proposed reduction in setups, identify the datum transfer it removes and any work that remains after unclamping. Check a flexible part after the holding forces are removed. Retain the finishing and inspection scope in the comparison, even when both offers name the same machine type.

sections.title: Reading the workshop setups
sections.html:
The turning, milling and multi-axis photographs below show cutting direction and workholding. A new part still needs its own dimensions and tolerances on the drawing.

A meaningful route review uses the complete model and drawing, finished and stock dimensions, material and weight. Those inputs connect the visible operation to working space, support, fixture clearance and the feature relationships that will be checked.

sections.title: Questions that remain before quotation
sections.html:
What can still require another setup on a five-axis machine?

The area used to hold the part may need finishing after release, and an underside feature may be hidden by that holding arrangement. The proposal should identify those remaining operations and their locating references.

What if the mating part needs a square internal corner?

The design review can consider a mating-part change, a permitted corner relief or a separately reviewed process. The drawing should identify the functional requirement so the proposed solution can be approved.

Can I request a quote before choosing the machine?

Yes. The complete part definition, material, finish, quantity and critical interfaces give LZZ a basis for reviewing the route. A process mandated by your own specification should be identified in that package.

What if the lowest quote uses a different process?

Review the surfaces completed, datum transfer, final condition and reported checks against the other offer. A different route can be reasonable when it includes the same accepted deliverable.

what-to-check-before-machining-a-cast-ho.seoTitle: Machining Cast Housings: Stock, Core Shift and Datums
what-to-check-before-machining-a-cast-ho.heading: Can the casting produce the finished housing?
what-to-check-before-machining-a-cast-ho.description: Review a cast housing before machining: available stock, core shift, locating contacts, finished bores and the records needed to release the blank.
what-to-check-before-machining-a-cast-ho.intro: Before committing a cast housing to machining, check that the blank contains the required finished geometry in the drawing's datum alignment, with enough wall remaining after cutting. A casting can look large enough and still leave too little material at a bore.
what-to-check-before-machining-a-cast-ho.libraryTitle: Checking a cast housing before machining
what-to-check-before-machining-a-cast-ho.summary: Evaluate the blank in the finished datum alignment before the first cut.
what-to-check-before-machining-a-cast-ho.reader_question: Can this supplied casting produce the required bores, faces and walls without moving the assembly interfaces?

sections.title: The blank and finished drawings answer different questions
sections.html:
Cast housing machining needs two controlled definitions. Casting drawing requirements describe what the foundry supplies, while the finished drawing describes the component that enters assembly. A cast opening can provide stock for a bearing bore, but the finished fit, axis and relationship to a mounting face still need their own requirements.

Both definitions belong in the machining review, with compatible revisions. Machined surfaces, retained cast surfaces and minimum finished walls need to be distinguishable. A finished solid alone can conceal the variation that the first setup must accommodate.

The ribbed cast-housing reference has a central opening beside surrounding walls and mounting features. Stock must remain around the full bore circumference without leaving the adjacent walls too thin. Specify the alloy, casting process and supplied condition with the blank drawing.

The Steel Founders' Society of America's ordering guidance describes identifying machined surfaces and locating datums for steel castings. Its steel allowance guidance cannot set the allowance for an aluminum or other casting process; that needs agreement for the actual blank.

Comparing a casting with a billet route

For a new pump or gearbox housing, the choice may be between finish-machining a near-net casting and machining from solid stock. The comparison needs the same finished interfaces and a complete definition of internal passages. A billet version that reproduces only the outside shape leaves the internal construction unresolved. Blank procurement, tooling and the quantity released also belong in the route comparison.

sections.title: Decide whether the blank is ready for cutting
sections.html:
Casting blank inspection starts with the blank identity, material condition and revision. For customer-supplied castings, retain the same incoming evidence so an unusable blank can be distinguished from work performed later. A layout with the blank located as proposed then shows whether the working features can be machined in the positions required by the drawing.

That layout includes internal stock, retained walls and stable contact locations. An ample outside envelope provides little reassurance if a core has moved the internal opening toward a finished wall. Defect criteria matter too: exposed porosity, a repaired region or a specified indication may require an authorized decision before work continues.

Three possible release decisions

FindingPractical next stepRecord
The required features have stock and the agreed criteria are metRelease under the incoming and first-part plan.Blank identity and the specified layout results.
A bore or wall cannot reach the released geometryHold for rejection or an approved design disposition.Affected feature, measured condition and authorized decision.
A repair or material indication needs approvalApply the purchasing criteria and responsible engineer's disposition.The finding, permitted action and required re-examination.

For customer-supplied castings, the quotation needs a clear boundary around incoming checks, unusable blanks and work already completed when a problem appears. Where the machining supplier arranges the blanks, foundry and machining requirements still need a common revision basis. A sample blank can help validate the layout and contact method before repeat deliveries.

Compare the actual blank in the proposed alignment

A nominal casting model overlaid with the finished CAD model is useful for design review. Incoming release also needs the actual blank evaluated at the locations required by the purchasing plan. Identify the cast contacts or datum targets used, then relate the measured stock distribution to the finished features.

A best-fit overlay can move the finished bore away from its required flange relationship. Keep that functional alignment fixed during the stock review unless a design change is approved. Use sections through the bore, nearby outside wall, flange and any critical internal passage to locate a shortage.

Agree layout coverage and allowance criteria with the foundry for the actual material and casting process. The SFSA ordering guide covers machined areas and locating information for steel castings.

sections.title: Core shift can consume the allowance on one side
sections.html:
Casting machining allowance is the material left for removal at the future surface. Casting core shift can redistribute that stock, so allowance must be evaluated in the required datum alignment. An average allowance or a generous dimension elsewhere on the blank can conceal a local shortage.

Consider an illustrative cross-section with a nominal 38 mm cast opening and a 40 mm finished bore sharing the intended center. That leaves 1 mm of radial stock. If the cast opening shifts 0.8 mm sideways, only 0.2 mm remains on the most exposed side before any allowance for variation or cleanup. At a 1.2 mm shift, that side extends 0.2 mm beyond the finished circle, so cutting cannot recover the intended surface there. These assumed dimensions illustrate the geometry; they are not recommended casting allowances.

Moving the finished bore toward the cast opening might improve local cleanup, but it also changes its relationship to the flange and mounting pattern. Where the drawing controls that relationship, such a move requires a design decision. Bearing bore cleanup must not consume the minimum finished wall thickness beside it. The adjacent outside wall therefore needs a separate stock and thickness check.

A future blank may need a revised allowance or casting process, agreed with the foundry against the finished definition. The current blank still needs its own disposition: suitable, acceptable under an authorized change, or unable to produce the released part.

sections.title: First-setup contacts and the stock left for later operations
sections.html:
Casting datum targets can identify the first-setup contacts when the route initially rests on cast surfaces. Where those contacts disappear during cutting, the first operation needs to create a stable face or bore while preserving stock for the remaining features.

Cast surface location can vary even where a patch looks flat. Cast housing bore alignment must remain related to the finished assembly references as the route transfers from those initial contacts to machined datums. Defined contact locations make the first setup repeatable, while support prevents a flexible wall from being forced into a temporary shape under clamping. Protected faces, lifting restrictions and unacceptable clamp-mark areas also affect the fixture.

The final datum scheme follows the assembly function. Temporary machining contacts provide a route to that result, and they may differ from the final inspection references. For related bores or a bore-to-flange relationship, the finished report needs to evaluate the drawing relationship after the relevant operations. Separate size results from unrelated setups leave that relationship unresolved.

The casting machining review uses the blank and finished geometry together to assess those transfers. Known contact restrictions are useful even when they do not appear in the nominal finished solid.

sections.title: Match the inspection to each interface
sections.html:
A bearing seat, seal land and mounting flange need different evidence. Bore size establishes the fit at the measured length; axis alignment and face orientation need the appropriate geometric checks. A sealing region may also need specified form and texture in the final surface condition.

Access can determine the checking sequence. An internal step may need measurement before an insert makes it inaccessible. Intersecting passages need an agreed internal edge and cleaning condition, along with a feasible way to evaluate it. Deburring, cleaning and coating belong in that sequence.

Dimensional acceptance and a pressure-boundary test serve different purposes. A pressure or leak test needs a defined medium, conditions, limits, responsible party and report when it forms part of the order. Its result cannot fill missing hole-position or bearing-fit data.

The drawing features guide connects local requirements to inspection records. Keeping the incoming blank layout alongside those finished results helps identify whether a later issue concerns the original stock, machining or another stage.

When a new indication appears during machining
FindingDecision to requestEvidence to keep
Surface indication away from a working interfaceAssess it under the agreed visual or examination criteria.Location, extent, blank identity and purchasing requirement.
Indication intersects a bearing bore or seal landAssess the fit, contact and remaining wall before continuing.Marked feature, measurements and required examination.
Possible pressure-boundary defectApply the specified examination or test and responsible engineering disposition.Method, limits and configuration covered.
Repair is proposedObtain approval for the repair and subsequent checks.Authorized procedure, affected region and re-examination record.

Casting porosity inspection follows the specified examination criteria when an indication is exposed. Cast repair approval should be obtained through the responsible disposition process, with the part kept on the applicable hold point. Removing more material to investigate can consume stock needed for the final surface, so agree the next operation with the party responsible for acceptance. A repair route belongs to the released record for that blank or batch.

sections.title: Keep the release basis available for the next batch
sections.html:
The production package brings together the blank and finished drawings, alloy and supplied condition, material records, stock checks and minimum walls. It also identifies the first locating contacts, final datums, protected surfaces, required examinations and any separate tests.

Casting first article inspection needs a defined scope and an identified sample. Casting supply traceability should retain the incoming blank, approved disposition and finished results that support that release. Batch sampling, traceability and authority for repairs or deviations should follow the same approved requirements. Model differences and accepted changes belong in the controlled specification so the next delivery can use them.

A visually similar replacement blank may use a different foundry route or treatment condition. Its contacts and stock distribution can differ from those used for first-part approval. Review those changes before applying the earlier layout and holding method to the replacement.

why-machined-plastic-parts-need-defined-.seoTitle: Measuring Machined Plastic Parts: Temperature, Support and Fit
why-machined-plastic-parts-need-defined-.heading: Why did the plastic part measure differently on arrival?
why-machined-plastic-parts-need-defined-.description: Make plastic-part measurements comparable by defining the polymer grade, temperature, conditioning, support and gauge contact used for acceptance.
why-machined-plastic-parts-need-defined-.intro: A sleeve can measure differently after transport even when both teams use the same type of gauge. Temperature, moisture history, support and contact force can change the comparison. Before changing the drawing or recutting the part, establish the material state and measurement setup behind each result.
why-machined-plastic-parts-need-defined-.summary: Define the material state and setup behind a plastic-part fit.
why-machined-plastic-parts-need-defined-.reader_question: How can supplier and receiving inspection measure a machined plastic part on a comparable basis?

sections.title: A tolerance needs a defined material state
sections.html:
Plastic machining tolerances need an acceptance state that can be reproduced. Plastic dimensional stability also depends on material and exposure, so a reading immediately after cutting describes the part at that moment. Receiving inspection may happen later, at another temperature and after a different moisture history. A meaningful acceptance condition identifies the state in which the working dimensions must meet the drawing.

Mitsubishi Chemical Group's dimensional-stability guidance describes temperature, moisture and internal stress as influences on machined plastics. The acceptance conditions need to reflect the actual material and application.

For a sleeve, both the bore-to-shaft clearance and the outside fit in the housing matter. A broad block may instead depend on the relationship between mounting faces. The drawing can define whether acceptance is free of restraint, supported at stated points or under a specified assembly restraint.

The perforated plastic strip illustrates a long form whose support affects hole-position measurement. The shafts and transparent parts in the plastic-parts collection have different fits and handling needs. Their common manufacturing method does not give them a common measurement setup.

sections.title: Use the data for the grade being ordered
sections.html:
POM, PTFE, nylon, PE and acrylic describe different material families. Fillers, stock form and processing history can introduce further differences within a family. A familiar color or trade description leaves those variables open.

Specify the exact engineering plastic grades and any fillers for the ordered components. Plastic stock condition and processing history also belong with that definition. Before approving a substitute, review its effect on fit and service behavior in the actual geometry. A suitable nominal property does not establish how the replacement will behave in a thin wall or long component.

Stress relief or annealing also needs a material-specific decision. Ensinger's discussion of annealing and machinability explains the relationship between internal stress, machining and dimensional stability. The relevant grade information and geometry should determine whether a treatment is appropriate and where it belongs in the route.

Choose material data around the fit

A bushing review needs the mating material, operating temperatures, moisture exposure and loaded condition. An acrylic cover may need appearance and edge handling alongside its mounting dimensions. Those are different acceptance tasks, even when both parts arrive in the same order.

Machined stock and injection-molded parts also have different manufacturing histories. A molded-part tolerance table cannot define the stock condition or measurement state for a cut sleeve. Transferring a fit between routes needs a review of the actual material and interfaces.

sections.title: Estimate thermal movement before tightening the fit
sections.html:
Plastic thermal expansion must be considered alongside movement of the mating shaft. Plastic bushing clearance depends on both size changes between inspection and service. A dimension accepted in a room-temperature inspection therefore needs to be considered alongside the operating fit.

For a freely supported part at an approximately uniform temperature, a first linear estimate is ΔL ≈ α × L × ΔT. Here, L is the original dimension, ΔT the temperature change and α the coefficient for the ordered grade over that range.

For an illustrative calculation only, assume α = 100 × 10⁻⁶ /°C, a 100 mm dimension and a 10°C rise. The estimated movement is 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 × 10 = 0.10 mm. The same assumptions over 400 mm give 0.40 mm. This assumed coefficient is not a specification for POM, PTFE, nylon or another grade; actual data must come from the selected material.

The simple estimate leaves moisture effects, machining stress and time-dependent deformation outside the calculation. Filled grades can also have directional properties, while restraint changes how expansion appears. For a sleeve installed in a metal housing, the assembled condition needs its own review rather than an unqualified free-expansion correction.

Clearance changes in the plastic bore and mating shaft

For a freely expanding bore and shaft at approximately uniform temperatures, a first estimate of clearance change is the bore's predicted diameter change minus the shaft's predicted diameter change. Use the ordered materials' coefficients over the relevant range and keep diametral clearance distinct from radial clearance.

A plastic sleeve pressed into a metal housing is restrained, so its free-expansion estimate cannot establish the installed bore size. A temperature gradient, moisture change or sustained load also takes the calculation beyond that simple model. The design needs the service fit considered separately from the agreed receiving-inspection state.

Where both are required, specify the room-temperature inspection diameter and hot running clearance at their respective stages, with the assembly geometry and limits for each.

sections.title: Support and contact can change the reading
sections.html:
Thin wall plastic inspection needs controlled support and contact. Plastic measurement force can deform a sleeve, so firm contact and a suitable lower-force method can give different bore readings on the same part. During machining, clamping can create a similar problem: the free shape after release may differ from the shape held against the fixture.

FeatureRelevant setupWhat the recorded condition resolves
Thin sleeveSupport, contact method and axial measuring locationsWhether results describe the same bore without different contact deformation.
Broad block or open pocketSupport points and permitted restraintWhether face relationships are measured in the required state.
Long stripOrientation, support spacing and handlingWhether distant holes are evaluated in a reproducible position.
Sensitive working surfacePermitted contact or an appropriate non-contact methodWhether the check can assess the feature without marking or deforming it.

An instrument name alone leaves much of that setup undefined. Recording how the part was supported and contacted lets the receiving team reproduce the check. With that information in place, the tolerance can reflect the assembly need instead of compensating for an unexplained measuring difference.

sections.title: Give in-process checks and release checks their own place
sections.html:
Plastic machining workholding must accommodate the support left as material is removed. Free-state plastic measurement can reveal a different shape after release, especially when a large pocket has been removed from one side of a blank. The supplier can assess the removal sequence, any intermediate rest and any appropriate material treatment for the shape being machined.

The drawing defines the final interfaces and material state. The supplier then selects tools and workholding to meet those requirements. A prescribed machining sequence belongs in the specification when the application requires it.

If acceptance follows conditioning, the earlier machining measurement remains an in-process result. The release result comes from the specified conditioned state. Labeling the two prevents an earlier reading from becoming the acceptance record by accident.

Wear, electrical insulation and sealing require their own operating criteria where they are included in the supply scope. The plastic machining review connects grade and geometry to the proposed dimensional checks; any application test still needs a defined method and responsibility.

sections.title: Make the first-part setup reproducible at receiving
sections.html:
Receiving inspection conditions should retain the exact grade, stock condition and relevant conditioning from the drawing and first-part record. Record the plastic inspection temperature with those results so the later comparison has an identifiable basis. The setup instruction then identifies free or restrained state, support positions, orientation, contact method and measuring locations. Material documents, sampling and any separate functional criteria complete the acceptance scope.

That receiving state also needs to make sense for the assembly. A part installed immediately after unpacking may experience conditions different from an agreed laboratory check. The design team can evaluate both, with a clear distinction between manufacturing acceptance and the intended service fit.

When the results still disagree

On a perforated strip, changed support can alter the measured relationship along its length. On a sleeve, contact loading can alter the apparent diameter. Match the conditions for one identified feature before deciding on a correction.

Retain the accepted setup and any unresolved items with the actual sample, as described in the prototype approval guide, before approving a repeat release.

Repeat one identified feature under matched conditions

  1. Confirm part identity, revision, exact grade and the measured region. Compare the same bore section or hole pair on the same part.
  2. Record the part temperature and relevant exposure history, including unpacking, storage and any agreed conditioning. Keep those observations with the readings.
  3. Reproduce orientation, supports and permitted restraint. Describe contact method and force where it affects a thin feature.
  4. Repeat the measurement under the agreed method before deciding on recutting, a material substitution or a tolerance change.

Ensinger's dimensional-stability guidance identifies material type, temperature, humidity and exposure duration as relevant influences on plastic part conditioning. For the selected nylon grade, review nylon moisture absorption against the actual fit and record the exposure history that affects the comparison. A low-water-absorption polymer may need different handling records. Use the grade's data to decide which conditions matter.

A plastic measurement disagreement that remains under matched conditions calls for both setups to be retained. Plastic part reinspection should investigate the instrument, method and material response before a dimensional correction is authorized. Record any approved conditioning procedure, including temperature, environment and duration or equilibrium criterion as applicable. There is no universal waiting time for every polymer and geometry; an instruction to wait overnight leaves those conditions undefined.

preparing-an-impeller-model-for-5-axis-m.seoTitle: Preparing an Impeller Model for 5-Axis Machining
preparing-an-impeller-model-for-5-axis-m.heading: An impeller model that machining and inspection can both use
preparing-an-impeller-model-for-5-axis-m.description: Prepare controlled blade, root and hub geometry for an impeller review, including cutter access, inspection coverage and separately specified rotor tests.
preparing-an-impeller-model-for-5-axis-m.intro: The difficult part of an impeller model is often inside the blade passage. Define the surface through the root, relate it to the hub and leave a feasible approach for both cutting and inspection.
preparing-an-impeller-model-for-5-axis-m.summary: Connect blade and hub geometry to tool access and finished-part evidence.
preparing-an-impeller-model-for-5-axis-m.reader_question: What must my impeller model and drawing define before a supplier can assess cutting and inspection?

sections.title: Keep blades, roots and hub in one controlled definition
sections.html:
An impeller CAD model must contain the approved blade and passage surfaces, their connection to the hub and the interfaces that locate the finished rotor. Check blade root geometry for missing or approximate faces before using that revision for programming or inspection.

The swept-blade impeller reference illustrates narrow passages around a central hub. Curvature, root geometry and hub access all affect the proposed route. Its photograph supplies geometry context; the new part's tolerances and operating requirements still come from its controlled definition.

Identify the governing model, part number, revision and units in the manufacturing package. The drawing adds datums, material condition, surface requirements and edge details that the model may not carry. Families of rotors need distinct part identities where hub dimensions, blade profiles or mounting features differ, since those changes can alter cutting and measurement.

Resolve a missing or inconsistent face before CAM

For a hypothetical gap near a blade root, mark the affected region and proposed repair. A repaired face can look smooth while changing the controlled blade or root geometry, so the design owner must approve that change. Keep the repair proposal and approved replacement file together under an identifiable revision, and use that released model for programming and later geometry comparison.

A neutral solid or surface model can be convenient for exchange. For a mesh or display-only file, the package should state its intended use and whether it is adequate for the required manufacturing and inspection. When files disagree, the supplier needs to know which one controls.

Check the manufacturing file before programming
File itemReview on the released modelDecision if it is unresolved
Units and orientationKnown dimensions, rotor axis and mounting reference.Resolve scale or coordinate differences with the design owner.
Blade and root surfacesComplete intended faces without missing patches or contradictory versions.Identify the region and approve a controlled repair.
Hub and mounting interfaceThe final bore, face and retention geometry.Reconcile the model with the drawing's fitted interface.
Repeated blades or variantsThe correct count, profile and named rotor variant.Release a distinct revision or part identity.

sections.title: Follow the complete tool assembly into the passage
sections.html:
Impeller tool access must include the cutter and holder throughout the passage. A tool holder collision with a neighboring blade can prevent a route even when the cutter tip reaches the root in CAD. The spindle approach, fixture, stock and rotating workpiece also need space throughout the operation. Passage depth, local curvature and hub height can all limit the available approach.

Sandvik Coromant's closed-pocket guidance uses blisk and impeller forms to explain how closed angles affect milling access. A particular rotor still needs a review of its complete surfaces and proposed holding arrangement.

Root radius and blade thickness are design features. A larger transition may offer tool access, but the permitted change needs an approved range or a design proposal. Likewise, a broad instruction to remove sharp edges can conflict with a controlled leading or trailing edge. The final profile and permitted edge preparation belong on the relevant regions.

An impeller machining fixture can use the hub or temporary stock while protecting the eventual mounting interface. Hub datum features for finished acceptance still need to follow the drawing rather than an assumed convenient machining contact.

Open and shrouded forms need different access reviews

An open impeller exposes passages from one side. A shrouded design can enclose surfaces and change the viable construction route. The package needs the full enclosed geometry and any proposed separate pieces or joining operations. A workable open-impeller setup cannot establish that the corresponding closed form is reachable.

sections.title: Let the cutting corridor determine the required motion
sections.html:
Indexed 3+2 work sets an orientation and holds it during the cut. Simultaneous five-axis work changes orientation as the path advances. A swept blade surface can create a need for changing access, especially when the holder has to clear both a neighboring blade and the hub.

For 5-axis impeller machining, follow the available cutting corridor through each passage. Indexed impeller machining can suit surfaces reachable from fixed directions; other regions may need a changing approach. Tool length, holder diameter, available support and rotary limits affect which orientations are practical. The process-selection guide explains the same distinction on other part forms.

CAM review needs the tool assembly, fixture and stock at each stage. A holder that clears at the passage entrance may approach a blade farther along the path. Machine travel and rotary limits need evaluation over that sequence as well.

Simulation evaluates the proposed cutting route. The finished-part inspection plan evaluates the resulting geometry. Keeping both attached to the same approved model lets the supplier and design team distinguish an access proposal from acceptance of a changed blade surface.

sections.title: Define which surfaces the inspection must establish
sections.html:
“Compare to CAD” leaves several decisions open. A blade profile result needs the controlling model, datums, evaluated regions and limits. Root regions, thin edges and tips can need particular attention because a general scan may leave them poorly covered.

RegionWorking requirementEvidence to agree
Blade surfaceControlled profileEvaluated areas, alignment and comparison with the approved model.
Root transitionDefined surface and permitted local changesA method that reaches and evaluates the specified root regions.
Hub bore and seating faceFit, axial location and relationship to the rotorSize and geometric results from the required datum setup.
Working edgesFinal profile, thickness or edge conditionLocal checks appropriate to the controlled sections.

An impeller blade profile result needs CAD comparison alignment that answers the drawing requirement. A favorable overall color plot can conceal a local region or evaluate the model from a different reference. The report needs to make its coverage and unevaluated areas clear.

Keep model, toolpath and inspection tolerances identifiable

The drawing's profile requirement defines acceptable part geometry. CAM settings control how the proposed path approximates its target, while a measurement comparison has its own alignment, coverage and evaluation settings. The same number entered in these different places does not make them equivalent.

Impeller root inspection should identify the regions evaluated and any areas the method cannot reach. Blade edge thickness and hub checks likewise need coverage suited to the controlled sections on the first sample. Retain local results alongside any overall deviation map. An alignment chosen only to minimise the overall mismatch can answer a different question from alignment to the functional hub references.

If the proposed method cannot measure a required root, agree an alternative method or obtain design approval for a changed requirement before machining the sample. A clear toolpath simulation does not verify an unmeasured finished surface.

sections.title: Geometry, balance and operating performance need separate evidence
sections.html:
The material definition includes alloy, condition, any required defect criteria and supporting records. Heat treatment or another process needs an agreed place in the route so final checks describe the relevant material and surface state. Those records should remain connected to the accepted part or batch.

Dimensional inspection establishes its listed geometry. Balancing establishes an agreed balance result for a named configuration, which may be an individual component or a larger rotor assembly. The procedure, criteria, permitted corrections and responsible party need their own agreement.

Impeller flow testing needs a defined setup, limits and responsibility, as do speed, pressure, efficiency or endurance checks. Retain the rotor test configuration so the result can be related to the actual component or assembly tested. A machined surface or a blade-profile report cannot establish those operating results. The quotation can identify which activities it includes and which are performed later by the customer or another qualified provider.

A change at a root, edge or hub returns to the design owner because its effects can extend beyond machining. The five-axis machining review can then assess the approved revision against surface access and the required finished checks.

Protect controlled geometry during any balance correction

Impeller dynamic balancing, where included, needs permitted balance correction regions and prohibited areas identified on the released definition. A correction at a hub pad has different design consequences from material removal at a blade edge or seal interface. Approval should cover the correction method and any dimensional checks required afterward.

Record the rotor configuration and completion stage with the result, including attached hardware or a later coating where relevant. If another party balances the rotor assembly, provide the component identity and geometric records that party needs. The quotation should state who performs each activity and who releases the completed configuration.

sections.title: Impeller model and inspection release checklist
sections.html:
The review package needs the complete controlled model and drawing, units and revision; exact material and treatment; blade, root, hub and mounting requirements; and the final edge and protected-surface definition. It should distinguish fixed geometry from features open to a manufacturability proposal.

Inspection datums, reported regions, proposed methods and first-part hold points complete the geometric scope. Quantity and repeat expectations establish the release basis. Any balance or operating test then has its own configuration, procedure and responsibility alongside that scope.

Consider an illustrative first sample supplied before a planned coating. Its dimensional results can support review of the uncoated geometry. Coating-dependent fit, final profile and any unperformed rotor tests remain identifiable open items. Batch release can then state exactly what has been accepted, under which revision and in which configuration, instead of treating one approval as evidence for every later stage.
