cnc-machining-cost-factors.seoTitle: CNC Machining Cost: What Changes the Price of a Part
cnc-machining-cost-factors.heading: What determines the cost of a CNC machined part?
cnc-machining-cost-factors.description: Understand how setup, geometry, material, tolerances and batch size affect CNC machining cost, with a worked example of setup cost per part.
cnc-machining-cost-factors.intro: The price in a CNC machining quotation covers the work needed to deliver an acceptable finished part. Some of that work happens once for the order; some repeats on every piece. The cost depends on which features and order choices change that work.
cnc-machining-cost-factors.summary: How setup, geometry and acceptance requirements affect the price.
cnc-machining-cost-factors.reader_question: Why does this part cost what it does, and which changes could reduce the price without losing its function?

sections.title: Where the money goes
sections.html:
CNC setup cost per part depends on how preparation is shared across the released quantity. CNC programming costs, tool selection and workholding preparation arise before the first usable part comes off the machine. Material, cutting, loading and the agreed checks then contribute to the cost of the pieces delivered. A prototype carries its preparation cost on very few parts; a batch can share some of that preparation.

Suppliers can include these costs in a unit price or list them separately. Either format can describe the same work. What matters is whether the price includes the specified stock, secondary operations, final treatment, inspection records and packing. Penta Precision's cost guide describes how setup and quantity affect a machining quotation.

A lower unit price can still mean a larger purchase

For an offer with setup listed separately, order total = setup + quantity × unit price + other separate charges. Costs already included in the unit price belong in that calculation once.

As a hypothetical example, assume a setup charge of $240 and a production price of $18 per part. One part costs $258; ten cost $420, or $42 each; fifty cost $1,140, or $22.80 each. These invented figures illustrate cost allocation, not LZZ pricing. The fifty-piece order has the lowest average price and the highest cash commitment. Its value depends on whether those pieces will be used before the design changes.

Once you have actual offers, the quotation comparison guide helps establish whether they cover equivalent work.

Separate one-off work from costs that return with each release

Repeat order machining costs can still include machine setup and a first-part check even when the CNC program is reused. Finishing batch charges also need a stated lot basis, especially when one purchase is split into several releases. Ask what each charge covers before treating the prototype preparation as a saving on every future order.

Cost basisTypical work to clarifyQuestion for the quotation
Initial preparationProgramming, dedicated fixture design and the agreed first-article documentation.Which items can be reused for an unchanged revision, and under what conditions?
Each pieceStock, loading, cutting, deburring and the specified individual checks.Which operations and materials are already included in the unit price?
Each production or finishing lotMachine setup, batch records, treatment preparation and packing as applicable.Would separate releases repeat any of these charges?
Delivered orderFreight and any separately quoted delivery services.What remains payable or arranged by the buyer at the named destination?

Suppliers group these costs differently. Count an included cost once. If a finishing or inspection charge applies per lot, confirm how the proposed quantity will be grouped.

sections.title: What quantity changes, and what it leaves unchanged
sections.html:
Prototype machining cost concentrates preparation on a small number of pieces. Small batch CNC machining cost can spread that work over more parts when they share one stable specification. It can also make a dedicated fixture or a different stock purchase worthwhile. The extra preparation must earn its cost back within the order or the agreed pattern of repeat releases.

Suppose, purely for comparison, that a different fixture adds $300 but saves $4 on each piece. The machining saving equals the extra preparation at 75 pieces: $300 ÷ $4 = 75. That calculation excludes stock, inspection, finishing and any price changes between quantities. It identifies a question for a quotation; it does not establish an economic batch size on its own.

Prices for realistic quantities such as 1, 10 and 50 pieces are useful when the material, released drawing and acceptance scope stay the same. Forecast demand can accompany those quantities, with the firm purchase identified separately. The prototype-to-batch guide explains the release decisions behind that distinction.

Earlier programs and fixtures may help a repeat order. Their usefulness depends on the current revision, fixture availability, material condition and required checks. A new fitted bore or a changed finish can alter the route even when the part looks familiar.

sections.title: Why a small part can take more work
sections.html:
Deep pocket machining cost follows the reach and support needed inside the recess. Internal corner machining cost can rise when a small radius restricts the usable cutter, even on a small block. The cutter needs room to reach the floor and corners, and the remaining material needs support while it is cut. Outside dimensions alone reveal little about that access.

A small internal radius may require a smaller tool. Combining it with a deep pocket can also require a long reach, a different sequence or additional passes. Where the corner provides clearance only, an approved relief or larger radius may simplify machining. Strength, sealing and assembly requirements still decide whether that change is acceptable. Protolabs' design guidance discusses small tools, pocket geometry and thin walls in cost reduction.

Features hidden by the first clamping arrangement can require another setup. Relocating and supporting the part takes work, particularly when a dimension connects features made in different orientations. A route with fewer setups may reduce handling while requiring a more elaborate fixture. The complete route and order quantity determine whether it saves money.

sections.title: The cost of locating a part again
sections.html:
The two-stage milling study records two operations on one component. On a new design, a second orientation can add locating, clamping and inspection work because the features made in each setup must retain their specified relationship.

A design change may be worth quoting if it gives the cutter access without disturbing the required relationships between features. It might remove a repositioning step, but a fit that depends on features machined in both orientations will still need locating and inspection. A revised quotation against the changed drawing shows whether the change reduces cost.

sections.title: Spend precision on the enclosure interfaces
sections.html:
A housing's sealing rim, fitted register and clearance cavity serve different purposes. Applying the same demanding tolerance and finish to all of them can add work that the assembly does not need. The pocketed enclosure study makes those different regions easy to see.

For a new enclosure, the useful review follows the mate: where the lid locates, which faces seal, where fasteners sit and which recesses simply leave room. Cosmetic requirements belong on the visible surfaces. Any relaxed limit needs design approval and must leave the necessary wall section, fit and sealing geometry intact.

The aluminum enclosure guide develops this review around particular corners, walls and interfaces. Those details give a supplier something specific to reprice.

sections.title: Price the whole cylindrical component
sections.html:
Turning can establish the main diameters and shoulders while a flat, slot or side hole requires secondary work. The turning-then-milling study illustrates that sequence.

The complete model and drawing let the quote cover both the off-axis feature and its required relationship to the working axis or shoulder. An estimate based only on the round profile can miss that preparation and inspection.

sections.title: The stock purchase behind the finished part
sections.html:
CNC machining material cost follows the stock purchased for the route. Billet stock size must cover the finished shape, machining allowance and the material needed for the planned holding method. A lightweight pocketed housing can begin as a much heavier block, so finished part weight alone cannot establish the stock purchase cost.

Grade and condition also influence the comparison. An alternative needs to meet the required load, exposure, electrical or thermal function and final treatment. The material and finish guide keeps those decisions connected. A separately priced alternative should name its exact designation and condition so its effect can be reviewed.

A casting introduces a different starting point. Its condition, allowance and usable locating surfaces affect the machining plan, as does responsibility for supplying the blanks. The casting-machining scope explains the information needed for that review.

sections.title: A tighter requirement changes how the part is made and accepted
sections.html:
Tight tolerance machining cost includes the route needed to make the feature reliably. Dimensional inspection costs also depend on the method and coverage needed to evaluate that specific fit or relationship. A hole pattern located from a mounting face raises a different task from checking a simple outside dimension. The cost follows the actual feature, access and evidence required.

Fit, sealing, location and movement explain where precision is useful. On other features, the responsible designer can assess whether a less demanding limit preserves function. The change belongs in the approved files before it becomes a pricing assumption.

Surface texture needs its own requirement. A size limit does not define roughness, and a polished appearance does not establish either. The drawing guide connects these characteristics to distinct checks, including whether they apply after treatment.

Report coverage also matters. A few measurements for an assembly trial and a feature-by-feature report are different deliverables. Identified features, sampling, methods and the required format give the quotation a defined inspection scope.

sections.title: Follow the cost through to the receiving condition
sections.html:
CNC surface finishing costs depend on the specified process, treated regions and acceptance scope. Machined parts shipping costs then follow the protection and delivery arrangements for that finished component. Treatment, masking and appearance references can affect both preparation and the checks needed on finished bores, threads or contact faces. Final dimensions need an agreed treatment state and allowance.

The accepted surface then needs to survive handling. Separation, thread protection, labels and records are part of the delivered order where specified. The packing and shipping guide helps connect those requirements to receiving.

Freight comparisons need the same destination, shipping basis and named place. Production completion and arrival are separate dates; clearance, duties, taxes and local delivery also need an identified responsible party. A quote that leaves those costs with the buyer can still be useful, provided the comparison accounts for that scope.

sections.title: Find a change that removes work
sections.html:
A useful cost review identifies a feature that can change and explains the work that change removes. A larger clearance radius may improve tool access. A revised nonfunctional surface limit may simplify finishing. Combining releases may share preparation, provided the design is stable enough to justify the larger purchase.

Each option has a boundary. Corner relief must leave the needed section and clearance; a tolerance change must preserve fit; a material alternative must meet the application and procurement requirements. A saving obtained by dropping a required report or treatment changes the deliverable and belongs visibly beside the original offer.

Keep the proposed geometry or specification change with its revised quotation. That makes it possible to choose an approved alternative and later order the same version. The quote comparison guide covers that purchasing record.

What a machining cost estimate can tell you

Record the material, stock size, geometry, quantity and finish used by a calculator. Those assumptions provide a starting point for drawing review of tool access, setup and inspection.

A CNC machining cost estimate based on a machining hourly rate needs a credible time allowance and a clear inclusion list. Milling a housing may involve roughing, wall finishing and a final fitted-bore check; a turned body may also need cross-hole machining. Rates alone cannot establish the relative cost of those finished parts.

The current model, controlled drawing and realistic quantities provide a starting point. Critical features, records and destination can be added using the RFQ brief.

Check which time the estimate includes

For a machined housing, spindle cutting time covers only part of the route. Loading, probing, tool changes, repositioning and deburring also take time. Check whether those operations sit within the quoted time or in separate setup and inspection charges.

If an estimate and a firm quotation differ, compare the stock size, number of holding positions, final treatment and report coverage first. Then ask which operation changed the time allowance. A proposed pocket radius or tolerance change should have its own approved drawing reference before its saving is accepted.

sections.title: Questions that come up before a firm quotation
sections.html:
Can I calculate a part price from the hourly rate?

Only when the time covers the operations being priced and the separately charged work is identified. Use the time-basis checks above to compare the estimate with a drawing-based quotation.

Why can two quotes differ after the drawing is fixed?

Suppliers can use different routes or price different inclusions. The same revision still needs the same grade, finish, quantity, acceptance records and delivery basis for a useful comparison. Written exceptions reveal which differences remain.

Will a repeat order cost the same as the prototype?

It needs a current quotation. Reusable preparation can change the cost, while quantity, material, finish or reporting can change too. The approved revision and intended release establish which work carries forward.

Can I obtain a budget while the design is still changing?

Function, approximate geometry, candidate materials and likely quantities can support a preliminary discussion. Its assumptions and open choices need to stay with the estimate. A settled drawing and order scope then provide the basis for a firm price.

rfq-checklist.seoTitle: CNC Machining RFQ Checklist: Files, Scope and Quantity
rfq-checklist.heading: Prepare a CNC machining RFQ
rfq-checklist.description: Prepare a CNC machining RFQ with controlled files, material, finish, quantity and acceptance requirements. Includes a copyable inquiry brief.
rfq-checklist.intro: A CNC machining RFQ gives the supplier a part definition, quantity and required delivery condition. The model explains the shape; material, local tolerances, finish and acceptance requirements explain what must be priced. Open decisions can be raised in the inquiry before the design is complete.
rfq-checklist.summary: The files and order details that make a quotation useful.
rfq-checklist.reader_question: What should I send so a supplier can quote the part I actually need?

sections.title: Give the geometry a controlled specification
sections.html:
CNC machining drawing requirements should be tied to the same part number, units and revision as the model. Use a STEP file for CNC machining to review shape and access. The controlled 2D drawing can carry fits, datums, thread details, sealing faces and acceptance notes. If they conflict, a named governing document or corrected release avoids two possible quotation bases.

A model alone can start a review. An enclosure cavity, for instance, may be clear while its lid fit and finished bore limits remain unspecified. The enclosure guide shows the interface details that make the difference. A model-based project can use another controlled requirements dataset, provided its authority and coverage are clear.

CNC inspection requirements belong in the inquiry when they affect acceptance. The first article report format, its coverage, methods, instrument range, calibration evidence and available documentation need agreement before ordering when required. Overall part and stock dimensions, and their weights if known, are also useful for multi-axis review.

When starting from a physical sample, the supplier needs to distinguish retained features from wear, damage and requested changes. Material and treatment require their own specification or supporting records. Drawings are optional in LZZ's inquiry form, so the first contact can explain the application and the information available now.

One useful section view can resolve an important assumption

For a pocketed housing, a section through the floor, walls and lid register can explain what the outside view hides. It can also identify faces that must be protected during clamping. A shaft or sleeve benefits from its mating component, working fit length and datum axis for runout.

A cast housing needs both blank and finished geometry, incoming checks and responsibility for supplying blanks. A plastic strip, block or sleeve needs the ordered grade, assembly condition and measurement support. These additions answer manufacturing or acceptance questions that repeated screenshots cannot settle.

Keep multiple part numbers distinguishable

A file list can pair each model and drawing with its part number, revision and quantity. For an assembly, a bill of materials distinguishes the machined components from purchased and customer-supplied items, and establishes whether assembly itself is included.

Superseded files can remain as history if they are clearly marked. The governing package needs to identify the version being quoted, so a familiar filename or a similar-looking component cannot quietly substitute for the intended release.

Use a file manifest for a multi-part CNC machining RFQ

A CNC RFQ file manifest can be a short spreadsheet or a table in the inquiry. For a multi-part machining RFQ, give each quoted item a row and check that its model, drawing, revision and quantity belong together. A folder containing several revisions is not a release instruction.

FieldSpecification and conflict to resolve
FilesPair the part number and revision with the model and drawing filenames. Resolve a STEP/PDF version mismatch before release.
ItemsGive the firm quantity per item. List assembly work and purchased components separately so one assembly quantity is not applied to every component.
StockName the material grade, condition and finish reference. Resolve any conflict between assembly notes and the individual part drawing.
DataIdentify critical features and the report or certificate format. State which features and delivery stage the record must cover.

Open the files once as a set before sending them. Check units, revision blocks and filenames against the manifest, and identify the governing requirement for any conflict. For a mating pair, include both relevant interfaces even if only one component is being quoted. The drawing requirements guide explains how to make those acceptance features identifiable.

sections.title: Describe the material and the final surface
sections.html:
The CNC material specification identifies the exact grade and condition being purchased. A machining surface finish specification separately identifies the treatment and the regions to which it applies. Required material records and permitted substitutes belong with that definition. Treatment needs its specification, applicable revision and coverage, including masks, edge conditions, cosmetic faces and required certificates.

A colour note leaves other requirements open. A sealing land may need a roughness limit, and a coated bore may need a finished size that the external appearance does not establish. Identifying the region and acceptance stage lets the supplier price the relevant work.

Open choices can be priced as named alternatives

If 6061 and 7075 are both candidates, the loads, environment and treatment requirements explain what will decide between them. Separate alternatives in the quotation keep the selection visible for engineering approval. An unresolved grade can then remain an explicit choice rather than turning into an undocumented assumption.

Keep unresolved requirements in one short list

Record RFQ open requirements with an owner and a decision point. For material substitution approval, name who can accept the proposed grade and condition before it enters the released specification. For example: “lid register dimensions after anodizing — design engineer to confirm before production release.” The supplier can identify whether a provisional assumption or a separately priced option is possible; neither should silently become the released specification.

Where a substitute is proposed, record its exact grade and condition, the reason for the change and who can approve it. Keep the original requirement beside the option. This makes the quote usable while the design is developing without presenting an unresolved choice as an accepted material change.

sections.title: State the release quantity and the required arrival
sections.html:
State the CNC machining order quantity against each part number. A repeat order forecast can help with planning, provided the firm quantity is identified separately. That distinction affects stock, fixtures and how much work the supplier is being asked to price now.

LZZ accepts orders from 1 piece. Its stated production period is 7 to 14 business days after drawing and order confirmation, including surface finishing; transit is additional. The quotation confirms the schedule for the agreed quantity and requirements.

A required arrival date and destination postcode let production and transport be considered together. The design-release date, quotation response deadline and any approval hold also affect the plan. Special protection, pack labels and the requested shipping basis establish what is needed at handover, including responsibility for customs, duties and taxes.

Show approval holds in the requested schedule

A first article approval hold belongs in the RFQ when the remaining pieces must wait for that decision. The requested machined parts delivery date should allow the supplier to assess the approval sequence as well as production and transit. Specify what must be submitted, who reviews it and whether any preparation may continue during that review. The prototype approval checklist helps define the evidence and the permitted next step.

Give separate dates for the quotation response, drawing release and required arrival. State whether partial delivery is useful and whether each shipment needs its own report package. A supplier can then respond to the actual sequence instead of interpreting a single “required date” as both production completion and arrival.

sections.title: A brief you can copy into the inquiry
sections.html:
Use this CNC machining RFQ template to record known requirements and open questions. Ask the supplier to state its machining quotation assumptions and identify any fields that still need a decision before production. Request an NDA before sharing confidential drawings if your project needs one.

Part number and drawing revision:
Units; attached 3D model and 2D drawing:
Material grade and condition:
Finish, masked areas and cosmetic faces:
Initial quantity; expected repeat quantity:
Critical features and acceptance limits:
Inspection records or certificates required:
Delivery destination and required arrival date:
Packing needs and requested shipping basis:
Open questions or permitted alternatives:

Before sending, check that every quoted item has a quantity and current file reference, that the requested arrival has a destination, and that unresolved requirements are listed openly. Ask the supplier to identify the assumptions and exclusions in its response. Use the quotation comparison guide when the offers arrive.

compare-cnc-machining-quotations.seoTitle: Compare CNC Machining Quotes: Scope and Order Cost
compare-cnc-machining-quotations.heading: How to compare CNC machining quotations
compare-cnc-machining-quotations.description: Compare CNC machining quotes for equivalent files, finishing, inspection and delivery. Work out order cost and resolve exclusions before supplier selection.
compare-cnc-machining-quotations.intro: To compare CNC machining quotes, first check that they cover the same finished work at the same release quantity. Start with the revision and supplied scope, then calculate the order total. If an operation or required report is missing, obtain a revised quotation before comparing totals.
compare-cnc-machining-quotations.summary: Resolve scope differences, then compare the cost of the order.
compare-cnc-machining-quotations.reader_question: Which quotation offers the best value for the finished parts and records I need?

sections.title: Put equivalent work beside equivalent work
sections.html:
A CNC machining quote comparison starts with the finished part requirements and deliverables. An anodized housing with a final bore report and an unfinished housing with in-process measurements are different offers even if they refer to the same CAD model.

ItemComparable basisDifference to resolve
Part and quantitySame part number, units, revision and firm quantity.Old files, variants or forecast quantities used for pricing.
Material and finishGrade, condition, treatment, masking and accepted final dimensions.Substitution or an operation left outside the price.
InspectionAgreed features, sampling, methods and record format.Missing reports, certificates or final-state checks.
ChargesUnit price plus all separately priced preparation and deliverables.First-order, recurring or conditional setup and tooling charges.
DeliveryProtection, labels, trade term, version and named place.Freight, clearance, duties, taxes or local delivery outside the price.
Timing and termsStart conditions, production endpoint, currency, payment and validity.Dispatch presented as arrival, expired pricing or unagreed change terms.

Similar terminology can hide different scope. A request for an inspection report still needs coverage; a quoted lead time needs a start and endpoint. Written assumptions make those differences visible while the choice can still be changed.

Mark missing scope before adding the prices

Record CNC quote exclusions beside the relevant requirement and quotation line. Keep unconfirmed quotation scope visible until the supplier clarifies what the price covers. Four statuses keep the comparison readable:

  • Included: the supplier identifies the work within the quoted price.
  • Separately priced: the work has a stated charge that must be added once.
  • Excluded: another party must provide it, with that arrangement identified.
  • Unconfirmed: the offer does not yet establish whether the work or cost is covered.

An unconfirmed material certificate, masked bore or delivery leg is not a zero-cost item. Ask for clarification or a revised offer. For a usable order total, keep the same currency, quantity and delivery destination, and show any currency conversion separately with its rate and date. Do not compare a tax-inclusive total with a tax-exclusive total without resolving the difference.

sections.title: Resolve the difference that explains the price
sections.html:
Separate CNC machining setup charges can change the machining order total even when the unit price looks lower. The following hypothetical ten-part order illustrates that difference. Assume Supplier A lists $120 setup plus $32 per part; Supplier B lists $43 per part with setup included. Before other charges, A totals $440 and B totals $430. These assumed figures are a purchasing example, not LZZ prices. At another quantity, either supplier may propose a different route and price.

The arithmetic is useful only after scope matches. If A includes anodizing and final bore inspection while B leaves them open, B needs an equivalent revised quotation or an agreed separate provider. An allowance invented by the buyer cannot establish who will complete the work or when it will finish. The material and finish requirements identify the condition being compared.

Preparation can be spread through unit prices or listed as programming, tooling and setup. First-order charges need a stated basis, as do any conditions for reuse on a repeat release. Quantity, revised geometry and report coverage can all change the work. The machining cost guide explains those drivers.

List machining material alternatives beside the original grade and their approval status. Tolerance change approval likewise needs the original limit, proposed limit and design decision kept together. The design owner can then assess the consequence instead of accepting a specification change through the price comparison. Earlier sample approval also needs review when its material or drawing changes.

A component price and a mechanism price cover different work

A component or assembly quotation for an indexing plunger should list the body, pin, spring and retaining items, then state whether assembly and defined functional checks are included. Keep that supplied-item list with the indexing plunger quotation. Where the customer performs later assembly or testing, identify the delivered configuration and responsibility for those operations. A reference photograph cannot establish that scope.

A quantity change can change the comparison

Under the same hypothetical rates above, eleven parts would total $472 from A and $473 from B. The apparent price order reverses because A has a fixed charge and a lower per-piece charge. This arithmetic assumes unchanged rates, identical scope and no extra charges; it is not an offer for eleven parts.

A quantity price comparison needs offers for quantities you could actually release. Request current CNC quotation unit rates and preparation charges at each quantity instead of extending an old ten-part price without confirmation. Finishing lots, stock purchases or a different fixture may change the quoted basis. A forecast for later parts also needs to be distinguished from the quantity purchased now; the prototype-to-small-batch guide covers that commitment.

sections.title: Make the accepted offer usable for the next order
sections.html:
Check CNC quotation validity when the offer is accepted. The purchase order specification should connect that quotation reference and date to the released files, quantity, delivery basis and approved exceptions. Currency, validity and payment stages explain the commercial decision. Terms for later design changes establish how price, schedule and acceptance will be reviewed.

Record the basis of each charge and approved alternative

A setup, tooling, inspection or freight line needs to identify the quantity and release it covers. Dedicated tooling also raises ownership, storage and reuse questions; the word "tooling" leaves those unanswered. An unchanged part on a later purchase still needs an identifiable baseline and current schedule.

A supplier's proposed material or process alternative can remain alongside the selected offer, with its approval status. When a drawing change affects the work, the comparison needs a new reference or revision. Purchasing and the supplier can then use the accepted scope without reconstructing the decision from email fragments.

Check the repeat-order terms before accepting tooling charges

CNC tooling ownership and the right to move a fixture need written terms. Fixture reuse conditions also need to be explicit; paying a tooling line alone does not describe those arrangements. Ask what was purchased, who retains it, how long it will be stored and whether maintenance or replacement is included. Record any agreed reuse conditions alongside the drawing revision.

Before issuing the purchase order, reconcile three items: the accepted quote and its exceptions, the released file package, and the quantity with its delivery and approval conditions. A later order can refer back to those records while obtaining current pricing and availability. The RFQ file checklist provides a practical starting point when the package needs updating.

machined-prototype-approval-checklist.seoTitle: CNC Prototype Approval: First Articles, Fit and Release
machined-prototype-approval-checklist.heading: What does prototype approval actually release?
machined-prototype-approval-checklist.description: Review a CNC prototype against its drawing and evaluation purpose. Separate first article results, fit trials, open issues and authorization for a batch.
machined-prototype-approval-checklist.intro: A prototype can answer a useful development question while other requirements remain unresolved. Approval needs to say what was checked, which configuration passed and what may happen next. A drawing inspection and an assembly trial often provide different parts of that evidence.
machined-prototype-approval-checklist.summary: Turn sample evidence into a clear approval or hold decision.
machined-prototype-approval-checklist.reader_question: How do I decide whether a prototype is acceptable and whether the next batch may proceed?

sections.title: Start with the decision the sample needs to support
sections.html:
Before CNC prototype approval, state the prototype evaluation purpose: checking board clearance, reviewing the finished appearance or completing a defined operating test. Select the mating components, fixtures and procedure for that task, and identify who can approve the result. Differences from production material or finish limit which conclusions the sample supports.

An uncoated enclosure can answer whether a board clears an internal wall. Where treatment affects the lid register or locating bore, their finished fits still need evaluation. The anodizing and masking guide explains the treatment boundaries that affect those interfaces.

For an indexing plunger, dimensions describe the components while an engagement and withdrawal trial evaluates movement in the agreed installed position. The mounting arrangement belongs with that result.

A successful assembly trial has a defined reach

Clearance holes can allow a flange to enter an assembly even while a specified hole-position check is unresolved. The circular hole-pattern guide separates hole size, pattern location and clocking.

For a simple hypothetical clearance example, a 10.20 mm opening around a 10.00 mm pin leaves 0.20 mm diametral clearance, or 0.10 mm radially when centred. That space can permit a particular trial without proving every drawing relationship. Actual limits, both component tolerances and the agreed test configuration still govern acceptance. This example is separate from the drawing exercise elsewhere on the site.

For a prototype fit test, record the actual mate and fixture, including temporary alternatives. In a prototype assembly test, record the installed configuration and interfaces tried. That record limits the approval to the arrangement actually tested.

sections.title: Read the evidence against the configuration tested
sections.html:
Part number, drawing revision and sample reference identify the article being evaluated. The material grade, condition and treatment identify its physical state. Approved alternatives or differences from the intended production part need to remain visible beside the results they affect.

Dimensional results show how the measured features compare with the drawing. Assembly observations describe the trial with the named mates; functional results need the agreed operating procedure and conditions. Cosmetic faces, burrs, edges and handling condition also belong in the review where acceptance depends on them. Photographs can document appearance issues and trial observations.

A useful inspection row can be traced back to the requirement

A first article inspection report uses drawing feature references to connect the required limit with the actual result, method and acceptance status. Sample identity, revision and measurement stage let another reviewer understand what that row establishes. Report coverage needs agreement before the part is made.

A photograph of a board installed in a housing can show its trial configuration. The mounting-hole pattern may still need the position results required by the drawing. Keeping these records identifiable allows both to support the approval without one being mistaken for the other.

Customer formats and named first-article standards carry specific requirements. Supplying them with the inquiry allows the supplier's scope to be agreed. The title "FAI report" alone cannot establish compliance with an unagreed standard.

An omitted check or missing material record remains an open item. Its effect on the next action depends on the requirement and the authorized decision; unrelated passing results do not close it.

Match the first article inspection report to the actual sample

Read a few critical rows from the requirement through to the physical part. Locate the feature on the drawing, confirm the sample and revision, and check that the measurement state matches the acceptance requirement. The drawing and inspection example shows how feature references connect the drawing to the record.

Prototype inspection coverage must include the features needed for the decision. A final state inspection of a fitted bore or sealing face remains open if the report omits that region or covers only an earlier treatment stage. Ask for the missing evidence by feature reference. If the trial uses a temporary mate, record its identity and which production interfaces it represents.

sections.title: Write a decision someone else can act on
sections.html:
The prototype approval record brings together the part and sample references, released revision, completed checks, supporting records and actual approver. Conditional prototype approval should identify the remaining hold and the work that may proceed. Its decision can be approved, approved with documented conditions, or not approved. Each unresolved item needs an identifiable next action, including whether another sample is required.

A condition must describe permitted work and the remaining hold. "Board clearance accepted; finished bore and lid fit pending" is more useful than "sample looks fine." It lets purchasing and the supplier distinguish the completed evaluation from the work still awaiting evidence.

A prototype design change belongs against the accepted sample baseline. Identify the sample reinspection scope from the affected features and tests before releasing the revised configuration. Their review identifies which earlier results still apply and which features need rechecking before the revised part is released.

Close an open item with evidence for that item

CaseAction and closing evidence
ValueFor an unexpected measurement, check the feature, datum, part state and method. Close the issue with a traceable recheck under the specified conditions and an explanation of any correction.
LimitFor a confirmed result outside the limit, identify the sample and hold the work covered by the approval decision. Record the authorized rework, replacement or acceptance of that specific deviation.
TestFor an unperformed test, identify what is missing and which operation remains on hold. Close it with the agreed result or an authorized change to the requirement.
ScopeFor limited approval, state the accepted purpose, permitted work and remaining hold. Identify the unresolved items and who can authorize the next release.

A prototype measurement recheck can resolve uncertainty in a reading; a confirmed out of tolerance prototype needs an authorized disposition. Accepting board clearance does not resolve a leaking joint or an unfinished fitted bore. Record a disposition for each issue. When an interface changes, list the affected dimensions and trials for the revised sample instead of repeating every earlier check automatically or carrying every earlier approval forward.

sections.title: Authorize the production quantity separately
sections.html:
A first article hold point defines where work waits for the recorded sample decision. Production quantity release needs authorization for the approved configuration and quantity, with the sampling plan, required records, packing and schedule recorded. Changes in material, finish or manufacturing route need review against the affected acceptance requirements.

A first-article hold also needs a practical boundary. The order can identify whether machining stops after the first parts and whether specified preparation may continue while review is pending. A missing cosmetic reference and an unresolved functional fit can justify different boundaries; the written release needs to say which applies.

For a revised sample, the changed features and retained evidence establish the next review scope. Production can then proceed only to the extent authorized by the recorded decision.

Use the small-batch release review to set the firm quantity, review any new workholding and decide what happens to earlier stock. Keep the signed or otherwise authorized approval record with that order so production receives a clear release instruction.

prototype-vs-small-batch-cnc.seoTitle: From CNC Prototype to Small Batch: Cost and Release
prototype-vs-small-batch-cnc.heading: Moving from a CNC prototype to a small batch
prototype-vs-small-batch-cnc.description: Plan a small CNC batch after prototype approval. Review the production revision, workholding, sampling, release quantity and the cost of later design changes.
prototype-vs-small-batch-cnc.intro: A prototype helps resolve a design question. A small CNC production batch commits material and machining to a released specification. Before placing that order, establish which sample results still apply, whether the production route will change and how many parts you can use at the current revision.
prototype-vs-small-batch-cnc.summary: Choose a release quantity and preserve the approved production requirements.
prototype-vs-small-batch-cnc.reader_question: What changes after prototype approval when I place a small production order?

sections.title: What changes between the sample and the batch?
sections.html:
Before moving a part from prototype to production machining, close or explicitly approve differences from the production specification. Small batch CNC machining may justify different workholding from the sample's temporary fixture. Keep any material alternative used for a limited prototype evaluation visible until it is approved for the batch, and release a baseline that describes the parts to be delivered.

DecisionPrototypeSmall batch
PurposeAnswer the stated fit, appearance or functional question.Deliver the released quantity to an approved specification.
RoutePrepare a suitable route for the sample quantity.Review reusable preparation and any fixture or sequence change.
Material and finishIdentify the evaluated state and its differences from production.Use the approved grade, condition, treatment, masks and final limits.
EvidenceRecord the sample checks, trials and open issues.Agree first-part holds, sampling, critical-feature results and batch records.
Commercial releasePrice the defined development parts.Confirm quantity, current price, production schedule and delivery scope.

LZZ accepts orders from 1 piece. Its stated production period is 7 to 14 business days after drawing and order confirmation, including finishing; transit is additional. The quotation confirms the schedule for the agreed quantity and requirements, including the effect of any approval hold.

sections.title: Carry the approved interfaces into the new route
sections.html:
A production workholding review asks which preparation can be reused across the quantity. CNC setup repeatability needs identifiable locating and clamping contacts that can be established for the intended releases. The finished relationships still follow the released drawing: a housing bore must retain its required relationship to the mounting face and hole pattern whichever fixture makes it. Critical datums and the setup sequence therefore belong in the batch review.

The approved material and surface specification also carries forward. Material records, treatment requirements, masking and dimensions after treatment define the final state. The batch inspection plan identifies sample selection, critical features, methods and reporting, including instrument documentation and records required at delivery.

For a plastic part, a new support arrangement or measurement time can change a reading. The plastic measurement guide explains the conditions that need to be consistent between production and receiving.

A similar-looking housing can contain a new interface

A revised lid register or connector opening may leave the outside shape nearly unchanged. Earlier approval remains tied to the old drawing and mating configuration. The next release needs to identify the affected rim, bore and mounting checks, including which earlier results remain useful.

The enclosure interface review helps locate these changes. A paired revised model and drawing, release quantity and disposition of earlier stock give the supplier a usable instruction. Repeating the part name does not communicate a revised fit.

Check the first part made with the production workholding

When a new fixture changes the locating or clamping surfaces, check the relationships that depend on those surfaces. For a housing, that may be the bore axis relative to the mounting face and hole pattern. A thin wall may also need checking after unclamping, in the state specified for acceptance.

First part inspection needs the critical features, method and any approval hold recorded before the run starts. A CNC batch sampling plan defines how later pieces will be selected and accepted after the first part. Specify the sample selection and acceptance criteria rather than relying on an unexplained percentage or the phrase “standard inspection.” The prototype and first-article approval guide explains how to record a limited release.

sections.title: Keep the sample, change and batch decisions connected
sections.html:
The sample record identifies its revision, material, finish, completed checks and open issues. A design-change record identifies the affected features and revised files, along with any effect on price, route, inspection or timing. The batch release then identifies the approved version, quantity, sampling and required delivery records.

These records can be short when the decision is simple. Their purpose is to let engineering, purchasing, production and receiving identify the same authorized work. A drawing revision or approved deviation should be traceable without relying on someone's memory of the sample discussion.

Find out how far the earlier revision has progressed

CNC drawing revision control needs to account for machining work in progress. Ask the supplier to identify the quantity at each stage: uncut stock, partly machined pieces, finished components awaiting treatment and treated parts. The drawing change then has something concrete to act on.

Machined parts rework depends on the material and operations still available. A larger opening might remain possible in an unfinished housing; superseded revision stock that needs missing material restored presents a different problem. Treatment can add another restriction. Ask for the proposed disposition and its effect on price, schedule and acceptance before authorizing rework. Keep superseded pieces identified and separate until that decision is recorded.

Update the model, drawing, order reference and any permitted deviation together. The person receiving the next batch should be able to distinguish an approved revised part from an older part that merely looks similar.

sections.title: Choose the quantity you can use at this revision
sections.html:
For low volume CNC machining, choose a CNC machining batch size that the current design and demand can support. A lower unit price can justify a larger order when those conditions are sufficiently stable. It also commits more parts to the current revision. If a mating component is still changing, the unused pieces may need review or rework before they can be used.

Put a number against each release

"Low volume" and "short run" do not establish a universal piece count. The order needs quantities per part number and intended release dates. Expected repeat demand helps the supplier consider fixtures, stock and finishing batches while remaining a forecast until incorporated into a purchase agreement.

For illustration, assume you need ten parts for a pilot and expect forty more after a design review. Releasing all fifty may share preparation, but it also commits the forty untested parts to the current design. Separate quotations for ten now and fifty now reveal the price of that choice; a forecast alone cannot establish it.

Repeat CNC machining orders need the accepted revision, material, finish and quantity kept with the current quote. Identify dedicated fixture charges and whether setup, inspection, packing and delivery are included or separately priced. Reusable preparation, dedicated fixtures and unused stock need an agreed basis. Arrangements for design changes, nonconforming parts and later releases stay with that accepted scope.

Distinguish a production release from a delivery call-off

OrderAuthorization and revision exposure
Per POSpecify the quantity and revision on each firm purchase. Later orders can use revised files, subject to a new quotation and schedule.
BatchFor staged delivery, specify the total quantity authorized for manufacture and each shipment quantity or date. Unshipped parts may already have been made to the released revision.
PlanFor a blanket arrangement or forecast, identify committed quantities, release instructions and any stock or fixture commitments. The agreement determines what can change; the forecast label alone does not settle liability.

Before committing material or machining, check the firm order vs forecast status of each quantity. If only ten pilot parts may be manufactured now, say so explicitly. A staged delivery schedule alone does not limit manufacture to the first shipment. Asking for ten delivered now and forty later can otherwise describe a fifty-part production release with two shipments. Confirm which arrangement the accepted quote and purchase agreement actually authorize.

custom-cnc-parts-shipping-checklist.seoTitle: CNC Parts Packaging and Shipping: Protect the Delivered Part
custom-cnc-parts-shipping-checklist.heading: Packaging and shipping CNC machined parts
custom-cnc-parts-shipping-checklist.description: Protect fitted, sealing and cosmetic surfaces in transit. Agree CNC part labels, packing lists, delivery responsibilities and the receiving inspection package.
custom-cnc-parts-shipping-checklist.intro: Shipping machined parts means preserving the condition accepted at final inspection and keeping the parts identifiable through transit and unpacking. Packaging must protect the working surfaces, while the shipping agreement establishes the destination and delivery responsibilities. Both need to be settled before dispatch.
custom-cnc-parts-shipping-checklist.summary: Protect the accepted surfaces and make the shipment traceable at receiving.
custom-cnc-parts-shipping-checklist.reader_question: How can I receive the correct finished parts with their surfaces, identity and records intact?

sections.title: Build the pack around the working surfaces
sections.html:
CNC parts packaging starts with the fitted journal, sealing rim and visible panel that must arrive usable. Precision parts shipping therefore needs a protection plan for the actual working surfaces and handling route. The packing plan identifies where supports may touch, which surfaces must remain separated and which threads or edges need protection. Cleanliness and corrosion-preservation requirements belong beside that surface information.

Protection has to survive handling

An aluminum housing can rest on permitted support faces while its sealing rim stays clear of adjacent pieces. Shaft journal protection needs defined support locations and restraint so the pack load does not pass through a slender section. Specify thread protection packaging separately for the exposed thread, including caps and separation from adjacent pieces. Those measures address contact damage; corrosion protection needs its own plan.

Cartons or wooden cases need a separation arrangement suited to the agreed pack weight and handling limits. For plastic components, the support and pack load also need to avoid changing the geometry that receiving will measure.

VCI packaging compatibility depends on the actual product, contact metals and finishes, storage conditions and removal requirements. Specify the required machined parts corrosion protection against those conditions before accepting a preservation method. The packaging supplier needs to confirm compatibility for that use. A bag name alone leaves those conditions unresolved.

Machined part identification should remain visible on the internal packs. Labels need the part number, revision, batch and quantity per package in the agreed format. That identity lets receiving connect similar-looking parts to the packing list while their working surfaces remain protected.

Check the pack with the protected features in view

Part featurePacking detail to confirmCheck before dispatch
Enclosure sealing rim or cosmetic facePermitted support faces and separation from adjacent parts.No hard contact or loose item can reach the protected surface during handling.
Shaft journal or exposed threadSupport positions, suitable sleeves or caps and restraint against movement.The load is carried by the intended supports, with no unprotected metal-to-metal contact.
Plastic sleeve or thin sectionSupport and stacking arrangement suited to the agreed receiving condition.Pack compression does not force the feature into a distorted position.

For a first shipment or an unfamiliar pack, request photographs showing the part supports and separation before the outer case is closed. Pictures of the closed carton alone cannot show the contact points. FedEx guidance for automotive and mechanical parts also addresses protection of threads, fittings and damage-prone surfaces; the actual pack still needs to suit your component and route.

sections.title: Work back from arrival without confusing it with completion
sections.html:
LZZ states production of 7 to 14 business days after drawing and order confirmation, including finishing. The quoted production lead time needs a clear start and completion point. Machined parts transit time is additional, and the actual quotation confirms the production schedule for the agreed order. Required dispatch and arrival dates, delivery address and receiving contact let the full journey be planned.

A hypothetical plan might allow ten business days for production, three for a buyer's review and five for transport and receiving. If those stages are sequential, the plan needs eighteen business days before any extra clearance allowance. These assumed intervals illustrate scheduling only; they are not LZZ or carrier commitments. Overlap, holidays and actual transport arrangements can change the dates.

The accepted quotation needs the trade term, version and named place, with responsibilities for transport, clearance, insurance, duties, taxes and local delivery. EXW, FOB or DDP applies only as agreed in that quotation. DDP is included only when specifically quoted.

Courier, air or sea arrangements depend on shipment size and destination. DHL, FedEx or UPS can be discussed for courier service; a named carrier alone does not establish the complete delivery basis.

Confirm the construction of wooden export packaging

ISPM 15 wood packaging requirements apply to regulated wood packaging material entering the United States. Regulated material must be treated and certified under that standard. Plywood export cases need their actual construction checked because solid-wood skids or dunnage can introduce a different requirement. The USDA APHIS guidance distinguishes that material from alternatives such as plywood and other processed wood.

The European Commission import guidance likewise distinguishes raw wood packaging from packaging made entirely from processed wood. A plywood case may still contain solid-wood skids, blocks or dunnage, so its name alone does not establish the treatment requirement. Confirm the actual construction, required marks and destination rules with the forwarder or importing authority before packing.

sections.title: Make the shipment understandable at receiving
sections.html:
A packing list, commercial invoice and shipment information need consistent order and part references. Material, treatment and dimensional records accompany the order where agreed. Any additional procurement or customs documents need review with the importing entity or freight forwarder because requirements depend on the destination and transaction.

Two freight prices can cover different obligations. ICC's Incoterms 2020 checklist explains the choice of rules and the import-clearance distinction between DAP and DDP. Check the named place and agreed responsibilities in the accepted quotation; a requested delivery term in the RFQ does not by itself settle them.

For plastic parts, receiving measurements need the agreed conditioning and support as well as the correct grade. Surface and thread protection should remain effective through unpacking. The specified material, finish and dimensional records need references that connect them to the actual delivery.

Preserve the evidence of an arrival discrepancy

Machined parts receiving inspection starts with the package condition and delivered identity. For a damaged sealing face, preserve transport damage evidence through photographs, the part reference and the agreed delivered-surface requirement. A plastic fit that measures differently calls for the ordered grade, conditioning, temperature, support and measurement locations. Similar parts that fail to match their assembly call for a revision and label check.

These comparisons help distinguish a handling problem, an identification error and a measurement-condition difference. They do not establish responsibility by themselves. Keeping the affected parts identifiable and unaltered allows the supplier and buyer to review the relevant records against the order.

Let the packing list do useful work

One line per part number and revision, with quantity and package reference, lets receiving reconcile the shipment. Internal labels matter when a carton contains several items; shape should not be the sorting method. Required inspection and material records need the corresponding part or batch references.

Reconcile the invoice, packing list and package labels

The commercial invoice and packing list serve different purposes. Split shipment documents must identify the quantity actually dispatched and the packages carrying it, with the remainder recorded separately. Trade.gov export-document guide describes the invoice as a transaction document and the packing list as the detail of the shipment. One should not be treated as a replacement for the other.

Before dispatch, reconcile the part numbers, revisions and shipped quantities against the purchase order. Match the package references and quantity per package, and check that net and gross weights use the stated units. Keep any parts still to follow outside the shipped quantity and identify their status separately. The importing entity or forwarder should confirm classification and destination-specific document requirements.

For receiving, have the packing list, released drawing, agreed inspection records and protected-surface requirements available before opening the pack. If a discrepancy appears, record which package and part are affected, retain the labels and photograph the relevant contact or damage area. Follow the agreed reporting process and time limits; this checklist does not establish a universal carrier-claim deadline.

critical-features-cnc-drawing.seoTitle: CNC Technical Drawings: Datums, Fits and Inspection
critical-features-cnc-drawing.heading: Turn the working interfaces into a CNC drawing
critical-features-cnc-drawing.description: Define CNC drawing datums, fits, hole relationships, threads and surface requirements. Follow a teaching example from feature callout to inspection hold.
critical-features-cnc-drawing.intro: A useful machining drawing explains how the part works with its neighbours and what counts as an acceptable result. Size, location, surface texture and final treatment answer different questions. Connecting each requirement to an identifiable feature makes the quotation and inspection easier to agree.
critical-features-cnc-drawing.summary: Connect functional interfaces to measurable drawing requirements.
critical-features-cnc-drawing.reader_question: Which requirements does my CNC drawing need so the finished part can be manufactured and accepted correctly?

sections.title: Begin at the interfaces that make the assembly work
sections.html:
Base CNC machining drawing requirements on the working interfaces. The datum reference frame should follow the references selected for the assembly; a locating bore has a different job from an outside clearance face. A mounting surface, shaft seat, sealing land or sliding face may need both a size limit and a defined relationship to other features.

The responsible design engineer selects datums, tolerances and the applicable drawing standard. ASME Y14.5 defines a system for expressing and interpreting geometric requirements on drawings and digital models. Naming the system and revision keeps the intended symbols and defaults identifiable.

In EX-MOUNT-01 below, underside A supports the plate and side faces B and C locate it. F1 identifies a bore size, F2 a centre distance and F3 a thickness. The feature references connect the sketch to its inspection exercise. Additional requirements would be needed for a complete production drawing.

sections.title: Keep each callout tied to the characteristic it controls
sections.html:
Bore and shaft limits establish accepted sizes. A fit also depends on the mating component's limits. Hole patterns and slots need their required location and orientation relative to the selected references; their diameters cannot establish that relationship.

Locating faces and axes provide the inspection references. Sealing faces need local surface requirements; cosmetic faces need an appearance reference. The drawing must also define threads, edges and treated regions where the model leaves them unresolved.

A balloon or feature number lets a report row point to one requirement. The exercise uses F1, F2 and F3. The number says which feature was checked; inspection frequency is a separate decision. One example reading, a sampled batch report and measurements on every piece cover different scopes.

Carry one characteristic into one report row

A ballooned drawing for inspection identifies each characteristic that must be evaluated. The dimensional inspection report should use those references as well as the physical feature name. One journal can have separate diameter, roughness and runout requirements. Reusing a single result for all three leaves the receiving team unable to tell which requirement was checked.

A practical link between the drawing and report
Drawing itemRecord alongside the resultReason
Bore diameterFeature number, size limits, measuring region and finished state.The reader can identify which section and condition the size describes.
Hole-pattern positionFeature number, tolerance frame, datum alignment and evaluated holes.A coordinate listing can be interpreted against the actual position requirement.
Local roughnessSurface region, parameter, applicable convention and measurement conditions.The result remains attached to the working land.
Accepted exceptionOriginal requirement, observed result and approval reference.A concession remains traceable when the drawing and report travel separately.

Keep the drawing revision in the report header and preserve characteristic numbers when practical during a revision. If a callout changes or is removed, identify that change in the new report. Receiving inspection can then distinguish a new requirement from an old measurement copied forward.

sections.title: Keep assembly references through the machining sequence
sections.html:
Machining datum transfer describes how the route carries a required relationship between operations. Cross-setup dimensions still follow the drawing datums for final acceptance, even when the supplier chooses different process references for workholding. When a bore and mounting face are made in different orientations, the route must preserve their required relationship across those operations.

The two-stage milling study shows the operation sequence and illustrates access to the top and side faces. A positional result still requires inspection evidence for that relationship.

For the teaching plate, A/B/C identify locating faces and F2 evaluates the illustrated centre distance. A production hole pattern may also need controls for position, orientation or form. Thin components may need a defined free or restrained inspection state.

On a circular flange, the seating face, locating bore and angular reference explain how the hole pattern is evaluated. A shaft or sleeve uses its working axis to connect fitted diameters, shoulders and runout.

sections.title: Size, form and position need separate reasoning
sections.html:
A passing diameter result says that the measured size met its limits. It leaves any unmeasured form or axis relationship unresolved. F1 in the exercise therefore cannot establish a positional requirement that the sketch never specified.

A fit clearance calculation needs both shaft and hole limits. The smallest and largest permitted mating sizes establish the corresponding size clearances under the stated assumptions. As a simple hypothetical limit calculation, a bore of 20.00 to 20.02 mm paired with a shaft of 19.96 to 19.98 mm gives diametral clearance from 0.02 mm to 0.06 mm. Those assumed limits illustrate the calculation only. They exclude form, alignment, temperature and treatment effects, and are separate from EX-MOUNT-01.

The actual application and drawing standard determine which controls are necessary. General tolerances help where their scope suits the function; local requirements carry the exceptions that the assembly needs.

sections.title: Specify texture where the surface needs it
sections.html:
A shaft can meet its diameter limit and still have an unsuitable working texture. A polished-looking face can also remain out of form. Each requirement needs the relevant characteristic and acceptance method.

Surface finish symbols need a stated drawing convention. Machining roughness requirements then identify the parameter, units, limit and actual area to measure. Ra describes the arithmetic mean of absolute profile deviations from the mean line. Rz describes profile height under the specified convention; definitions vary across standard editions. A universal conversion multiplier is unsuitable for acceptance.

Mitutoyo's surface-roughness guide explains profile parameters, filtering and measurement lengths under the editions it cites. The drawing's applicable standard and revision govern the part. Measurement direction and stylus access can matter on a small or interrupted land, so those conditions need consideration with the limit.

Treatment introduces a measurement-stage question. The material and finish guide follows preparation and treatment while keeping texture separate from colour, gloss and permitted marks. A demanding roughness limit on every surface can add work where an ordinary clearance surface needs no such control.

sections.title: Define the details that disappear in an outside view
sections.html:
A thread designation needs the system, size and class. Blind thread depth must identify the usable full thread; cross-hole deburring requirements separately address the internal edges where passages intersect. Drill depth describes a different extent. An insert has its own specification and acceptance requirements.

Blind and intersecting holes can hide edges that affect function. A fluid passage may require a different burr and cleanliness condition from an ordinary fastener hole. Verification needs to remain possible before a later operation closes access.

Edge notes need to preserve functional shape: defined chamfers or radii where size matters, retained sharp edges where required and local restrictions around seals or shoulders. An internal corner needs a permitted radius or relief suited to both the mate and the available tools. The process-selection guide relates corner geometry to depth and support.

A threaded fitting also needs its sealing geometry. Thread gauging evaluates the specified thread. Leakage performance needs an agreed test configuration, limits and responsibility.

sections.title: Apply the interface review to the complete part
sections.html:
A cylindrical body can need a side hole or milled flat after turning. In the turning-then-milling study, that second operation helps explain why the side feature may need a relationship to the working axis, shoulder or orientation feature. The drawing establishes it; the supplier selects the holding sequence.

The pocketed housing study directs attention to the cover face, locating bore and mounting pattern. Clearance recesses and cosmetic areas have different jobs. Finishing needs to preserve the required interfaces in the accepted state.

sections.title: Match the inspection method to the drawing requirement
sections.html:
Critical feature inspection distinguishes bore size, location and surface texture because they require different checks. A CMM inspection plan should identify which of those characteristics it evaluates and how the drawing references are established. A CMM may suit selected feature relationships; choosing it still requires a check of access, instrument range, datum setup, support and measurement uncertainty for each characteristic.

The agreed plan needs the feature and characteristic, required method and reporting, inspection stage and frequency. First articles, sampled production and every-part checks are separate scopes. Calibration, traceability and other test records belong in the plan when required for the order.

The teaching inspection sheet illustrates the release consequence. F3 reads 12.08 mm against limits of 11.95 to 12.05 mm. It exceeds the upper limit by 0.03 mm, so release is held even though F1 and F2 pass their numerical comparisons. Those readings are teaching data, not a complete inspection or proof that a particular instrument suits a production requirement.

sections.title: Record the condition in which the part was measured
sections.html:
A treatment can alter the surface being accepted. The drawing must identify the coated and masked regions and state whether limits apply before treatment, after treatment or at both stages. For flexible components, free and restrained readings can differ. Material, temperature and conditioning may also matter to a working fit.

The teaching plate uses the final machined condition without a treatment allowance. Its exercise cannot establish the result of a later coating. Similarly, an uncoated sample supports only its recorded configuration and checks; the prototype approval guide keeps those limits with the decision.

Make the final result identifiable

A bore measured during machining and after treatment can retain the same feature number with a different stage on each row. If a later process changes the surface, the earlier reading remains process evidence while the finished dimension needs its required final check.

For a coated or masked production fit, define the final limits and checking plan at the boundaries identified in the anodizing masking guide.

sections.title: Release files that describe one part
sections.html:
Part number, units and revision connect the model to the drawing. A governing document or controlled model-based dataset establishes authority. Material grade and condition, finish, masks, acceptance stage and required records complete the specification alongside applicable standards, traceability, end-use and export requirements.

The inspection scope includes dimensional, appearance and functional checks where required, with frequency, methods and available report format agreed before machining. A revised package identifies changed features and their effects on price, route, sample approval and repeat production. Accepted deviations need their approval reference.

Use general notes within their stated scope

A general tolerance covers the characteristics and conditions it names. A local fit limit, thread designation or geometric control remains necessary on a feature whose function needs it. Conflicting notes need correction in the controlled files so the requirement remains clear when separated from the quotation email.

The drawing standard, control frame and datum references work together. The bolt-hole pattern example shows why diameter and position need distinct evidence.

Resolve model and drawing conflicts before release

Drawing revision control keeps the model, drawing and inspection request on one released basis. Resolve STEP and PDF conflicts before manufacture; a nominal model and permitted limits in the drawing can work together under an identified governing specification. If the nominal diameter, unit system or hole count differs, correct the controlled package and identify the replacement files before machining.

For an inch drawing exchanged with a metric model, state the governing units and keep the tolerances in the approved system. Converting a nominal dimension in a CAD viewer does not establish how a tolerance was intended to convert. A marked discrepancy list should identify the affected callout, the controlling requirement and the person approving the correction.

Cite the applicable standard and edition on the released drawing; the ASME Y14.5 overview describes the standard's scope.

sections.title: Before the specification is complete
sections.html:
Can I start with a STEP file?

Yes. It supports geometry and access review. Material, tolerance, finish and acceptance information absent from it still needs a controlled specification before manufacture. A model-based project can use an identified requirements dataset.

Can the supplier propose different datums?

Access or measurement concerns can prompt a proposal. The responsible designer assesses the assembly consequences and approves the revised requirement before it is used in production.

Does approving a sample approve later batches?

Approval covers the recorded configuration and checks. Later releases still need the approved revision, material, finish and inspection plan, with changed or unresolved requirements reviewed.
